basis: The earlier graphics-effect name was still too broad: every dispatch target writes palette RAM, and the alleged scroll and tile handlers only change color words.
The selector word is loaded as a stage-configuration field and written by stage/camera setup code.
The only direct call is one step in the main gameplay rendering/effect chain, not the player state update.
The adjacent selector dispatches only palette fade and palette-update handlers.
It is called from the same gameplay graphics/effect chain as the primary dispatcher.
The payload is exactly 16 Mega Drive color words.
UI_InitializeSEGAScreen copies all 32 bytes into palette RAM immediately before loading sega_tiles.
Called once a frame from ZLeoEnding_UpdateScene. State zero skips both the scroll integration and the player placement, so the first frame runs the intro before anything moves.

The state index is SharedPatternRow0Long0 at $FF9400, not an object field, so this whole sequence keeps its state machine in the shared pattern scratch area: the index at +0, its timer at +2, the camera scroll rate at Long2+2, and the particle parameters across Long4 to Long7.
Nineteen self-relative words. Every state advances by two and never branches back, so the sequence is strictly linear and ends parked on the idle entry.

It builds a type-$10 object at the head of Entity_ObjectPool, which is the object the PrimaryEntity RAM names address. Type $10 is index 4 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, Entity_NullUpdateHandler4, so the object never updates itself and serves only as a moving marker.
The routine spawns particles and counts down a $40-frame timer. It touches no palette at all, which is what the former PaletteWait name claimed.
The counting frames return here; the last one starts the marker moving at four pixels a frame and spawns the impact object.
The test is cmpi.w against PrimaryEntityXPos, the marker X, not a camera Y as the comment claimed. It waits for the marker to reach $1E0, then stops it and arms the next $40-frame timer.
The frames before the marker arrives return here.
A bare countdown that keeps spawning particles, the shape most states in this sequence share.
The Z-Leo particle wait returns here while SharedPatternRow0Long0+2 is nonzero after decrement; zero advances the sequence state first.

This one really is the camera: Boss_ZLeoUpdateScroll adds SharedPatternRow0Long2+2 to PrimaryCameraXPosition every frame, and this state is what accelerates that rate. It also subtracts the same rate from the particle emitter origin, so the emitter stays fixed in world space while the camera moves.
Once the emitter origin has scrolled below $60 it is re-seeded at $160 with a wider spread, so the effect restarts at the other side rather than running off screen.
The rate rises by $800 a frame and the state ends on the exact frame it equals $80000, a compare for equality rather than a threshold, so the acceleration must divide evenly into the target.
Every frame short of the exact rate returns here.
It waits for the marker to fall back to X $120 or below, then copies the camera scroll rate into the marker velocity so the two move together.
The frames above the threshold return here.
It raises the per-frame particle count from one to two and re-seeds the emitter, then arms an $80-frame window.
The burst runs for its whole window and re-arms the same $80 for the next state rather than clearing it.
The Z-Leo burst wait returns here while SharedPatternRow0Long0+2 is nonzero; zero reloads it with $80 and advances sequence state.
It clears bit 0 of the marker flags and installs a leftward $20000, which is what sends the marker back the way it came.
The frames before the reversal return here.
The bit-7 test is a byte operation on the top byte of the marker velocity long, so it is a sign test: $1000 is added each frame until the velocity turns positive, and the turn is marked with SFX $D5.
The still-negative frames return here.
It keeps accelerating the marker and waits for it to reach X $1E0 again, the same value the early wait used, then steps the particle count up by one.
The frames before the marker arrives return here.
After its own $80-frame delay it sets the per-frame particle count to four outright rather than stepping it.
The Z-Leo mode-change delay returns here while SharedPatternRow0Long0+2 is nonzero; zero sets particle mode 4 and advances state.
A bare countdown at four particles a frame, the densest point of the effect.
The Z-Leo mode-4 wait returns here while SharedPatternRow0Long0+2 is nonzero; zero advances sequence state.
It arms $40 frames and advances in the same frame, so it is a one-frame setup state rather than a wait.
It clears the timer on the last frame, which is what lets the fade state reuse the same word as a fade index starting from zero.
The Z-Leo final delay returns here while SharedPatternRow0Long0+2 is nonzero; zero clears the timer and advances state.
The fade index advances only on frames where bits 0 and 1 of the VBlank counter are both clear, so it steps once every four frames, and every other frame spawns particles instead.
It clears $20 long words of PaletteShadowBuffer, the whole shadow palette, once the fade index passes $E.
The frames still fading return here.
The three frames in four that do not step the fade still emit particles, so the effect does not stall during the fade.
It holds the fade at its final index $E for $80 frames, then stops the camera scroll and the particle emitter together.
The holding frames return here.
The fade index now counts down on the same one-in-four cadence, and reaching negative sets GameModeIndex to $8C, which is what leaves the sequence.
Both skipped frames and counting frames return here.

The nineteenth and last state, and genuinely entered: the exit state advances into it after setting the game mode, so the controller parks here until the mode change takes effect. Its address comes from build/main.lst, because nullsub names carry a counter rather than an address.
It masks the index to $E, so the caller can pass any value and only the even steps 0 to $E reach Gfx_ApplyPaletteFade. Both callers are in this module.
The routine adds the Z-Leo velocity field to the horizontal scroll accumulator.
It neither reads nor writes palette memory.

Zero references of any kind: the only mentions of the entry label are its own definition and the cross-reference comments its four sub-labels carry, there is no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in rts so it cannot be fallen into. It moves PlayerXPosition and PlayerYPosition by four a frame from the held D-pad, which is the player object and not a camera as the former Debug name claimed.
Left is tested first, so holding both directions would move the player left.
The bit order is the standard pad layout: 0 up, 1 down, 2 left, 3 right.
The vertical pair mirrors the horizontal one exactly.
All four directions converge on this return.

Zero references of any kind, no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in rts so it cannot be fallen into. Like its live sibling it would write PlayerXPosition and PlayerYPosition, here from two sine phases advancing at four and two units a frame scaled by $40 and $20 around a fixed centre, so it is an orbit of the player object rather than of a camera. This record supersedes the earlier confirmation.

It writes PlayerXPosition and PlayerYPosition from the marker object position and sets bit 7 of the player flag word while the marker X stays between $80 and $1C0. It touches no camera field at all: the camera in this sequence is moved by Boss_ZLeoUpdateScroll, which adds the scroll rate straight into PrimaryCameraXPosition. This record supersedes the earlier confirmation, which was made before the marker object and the camera scroll were told apart.

Outside the bounds it parks the player at X $60 and clears bit 7 of the player flag word. Bit 7 of that high byte is the visibility bit: every visible sprite word in this codebase has it set and the hidden $1000 value has it clear, so the player is hidden while the marker is off the active span.
The routine allocates sprite objects, assigns randomized positions and velocity, and selects sprite frame pointers.
It emits periodic sound effects after the particle loop.
Direct writes in its particle loop populate allocated object X/Y positions, horizontal velocity, and animation pointer; its post-loop side effect is a queued sound request.

Each particle takes its spread from a mask in SharedPatternRow0Long5+2 and Long6, centred by halving the mask plus one, then adds one of four fixed offsets chosen by two random bits. Its horizontal velocity is the camera scroll rate halved, so the particles drift with the camera at half speed.
From state $18 onward the periodic sound changes from $30 to $2F, so the last two states of the sequence sound different.
The sound is gated by a random value masked with SharedPatternRow0Long7, so it fires on roughly one frame in eight rather than on a timer.
A zero particle count, a full object pool and the off-sound frames all share this return.
Four words, $20, 0, $FFE0, 0, indexed by two random bits doubled, so the horizontal jitter is plus or minus $20 on half the particles.
The companion four words, 0, $A, $FFF0, 0, indexed by the same random pair, so the two offsets are always taken together and the four combinations form a small diamond.
Eight long pointers over six distinct animations: SharedCombatSpriteAnimation03 appears twice and 00 and 02 appear twice each, so the random draw is not uniform across the six.
The routine initializes one object slot from the active Z-Leo object's position and sprite attributes.
It plays a sound effect and performs no tilemap transfer.
The routine advances an accumulator and converts it to a bounded range.
It tail-calls the shared effect-pattern buffer filler and does not update entity coordinates.
The routine advances a second accumulator and tail-calls the effect-pattern buffer filler when the boss is active.

The routine updates ShieldViperEffectStepB and ShieldViperEffectPhaseB, then either returns on boss-status flags or tail-branches to Boss_ShieldViperFillPatternRange; its imported palette-update name was false.
The routine mirrors the phase-B accumulator and pattern-fill behavior using a third state field.
It performs no object destruction or resource cleanup.
The routine writes zero across all 96 longwords of the effect-pattern buffer.
It neither allocates nor updates a projectile.
The routine fills a caller-selected range in the 96-entry effect-pattern buffer.
Its output is consumed by rendering transfer code rather than a projectile spawner.
The routine prepares the effect-pattern workspace and tail-calls the shared transfer primitive.
It does not perform shooting logic.
The routine builds collision lists and invokes player, weapon, terrain, special-attack, and platform collision passes.
It is called by the general gameplay update loop and is not owned by one boss.

The merge point of the two effect-pool bases. EffectCollisionOddStart is SharedEffectObjectPool plus $60, exactly one object, and every loop that uses the base steps by $C0, which is two objects, so the two bases split an eight-slot pool into its even and its odd halves and each half is tested on alternate frames.

The only writer of DebugResourceRefill that sets it is the debug menu, which steps it by two; every other site clears it. So the branch is live but reachable only through the debug menu, and it refills both the health and the stage timer.
Both the frozen-frame exit and the ordinary end of the update share this return.
The routine scans the complete object pool and classifies entries into five lists according to collision flags.
Several lists are consumed by player weapons, moving platforms, and targeting code, not only enemy logic.
Sixty slots of the object pool at a $60 stride, and one pass builds all five lists plus the pickup count, so the flag byte $21 is read once per object per frame.

The primary list is the only one that is halved: an object qualifies on a frame whose low bit matches the low bit of its own slot index, so each primary collider is listed every other frame and the player check sees half the objects per frame.
Bits 1 and 6 of $21 are the primary-collider mask, and bit 5 of $23 additionally counts the object as an active pickup.

The primary box is cached at $3C and $3E for the horizontal edges, from the $2E and $2F offsets, and at $38 and $3A for the vertical, from $2C and $2D. Collision_CheckPlayerAgainstHostiles reads exactly those four fields.

Bits 4 and 7 of $21 are the target mask, and bit 4 on its own also adds the object to the lock-on list, which is the same bit both damage paths later test to decide whether a hit goes to the boss health.
The target box is a second, separate cache at $34, $36, $30 and $32, built from the $2A, $2B, $28 and $29 offsets, so an object can present a different box to weapons than it does to the player.
Bit 5 of $21. Before listing the platform it copies the previous position from $48 and $4A into $4C and $4E and stores the current one, so the rider code can take the delta.
Bit 0 of $21 is the player-weapon mask, the last of the five lists.
Both an empty slot and a fully processed one converge here.

It probes one point per slot, the object centre, not several, so the multi-point comment was wrong. Four slots at a $C0 stride from the alternating base, and it reads the same $FFFF0000 tilemap and $FFFF7800 angle buffer that Collision_CheckTerrainTile uses.
A slot qualifies only while bit 6 of $21 is set and bit 6 of $23 is clear, and a hit swaps them, so each effect object is stopped by terrain exactly once.
An empty slot, a disqualified slot, an empty tile and an angle below 4 all converge here, so only angles 4 and above count as solid.
The outer loop scans four entries in the alternating weapon-effect pool at FFBFC0/FFC020.
On overlap it subtracts projectile damage from target health and handles target defeat or hit scoring.
d5 is loaded with 4 here and used as a register bit index later, which is what makes bit 4 of $21 the boss-target test.
Four slots at a $C0 stride from the alternating base, the same half-pool walk the terrain check uses.
The weapon box is a fixed eight pixels around its own position rather than the cached bounds, and it is tested against the target box at $34, $36, $32 and $30.
All four rejections converge on the loop tail.
Every resolved hit jumps here rather than back to the target loop, so one weapon slot lands at most one hit per frame.

This is the boss path, not a generic flagged one: everything below it reads and writes BossHealth, BossColorEffectFlags and the boss counters. The guard is that bit 2 of BossColorEffectFlags forces it through even at zero health.
A weapon with bit 1 of $23 set only damages the one object recorded in WeaponTargetOrFrame, which is how a locked shot ignores everything it passes through.

Three separate conditions divert to the blocked response: bit 1 of BossColorEffectFlags, bit 4 of the target $23, and any overlap between the low nibbles of the two objects $23 bytes, which is an element or armour match.
The score is awarded only when bit 7 of the weapon $23 is clear, so some weapons hit for damage without scoring.

Damage is the weapon $26 multiplied by the target $24, and the weapon $26 is then set to $FFFF, which is how one projectile is spent. On reaching zero the routine clears the health, the maximum, the colour flags and both combat counters together.
The ordinary path subtracts the weapon $26 straight from the target $24 with no multiply, and a negative target health is carried back into the weapon $26 so the overkill is refunded to the shot.
Bit 7 of the target $23 suppresses the destroyed-enemy tally, so scenery and parts do not count toward the results screen.
A surviving target scores $21 packed BCD against the $11 the boss path awards.
A blocked shot clears its own collision bit and overwrites its $23 with $50, and marks the target with bits 3 and 0, which is the deflection feedback rather than damage.
The fixed collision box is derived from the player object at FFA400.
The routine scans the primary hostile list and applies resource damage and response state to the player.
The player box is built from the $2A, $2B, $28 and $29 offsets, the same fields that feed the target box of every other object.
It walks the primary list, which the builder halves by frame parity, so the player is tested against half the colliders each frame.
Bit 5 of the target $23 marks a pickup: it gets bit 7 of $22 set and is skipped, so pickups share the list with hazards and are separated here.

The clamp is the mechanic: damage taken at exactly one point of health kills, and any other damage that would go below zero leaves the player on one. So no single hit can kill outright unless the player is already at one.
Objects without bit 6 of $21 only bump: they need bit 1 as well, the cooldown must have wrapped, and bit 0 of the player $21 must still be set.
It clears bit 0 of the player $21, which is what makes the contact single-shot until something sets it again.
Every rejection and every non-damaging contact converges here.
The restriction flag, an empty player flag byte, an empty list and the loop end all share this return.
The damage tally is a packed BCD increment through abcd with a saturating $9999 ceiling, so it counts hits taken rather than points lost.

The knockback is the whole $18 long of the hostile, copied straight into PlayerKnockbackXVel, and the displayed delta is the damage with bit 15 set for a $30-frame window. Bit 1 of the hostile $21 ends the routine here, so a contact-damage source causes no freeze and no stun.

The bounds above it are difficulty-scaled and the test is tst.w, a word read of DifficultyMode, so unlike the six tst.b sites in the weapon code this one works: difficulty 0 gives a $20 to $78 window and any other difficulty halves it to $10 to $3C.
The upper half of the same clamp.
Damage inside the window is stored unchanged, so the stun length in $5E is the damage clamped to the difficulty window.
The contact-damage exit shares this return with the clamp.
The routine constructs a collision box around the dedicated object at FFC5C0 and tests two target lists.
That object is initialized by player dash, projectile, and Z-Leo impact code; the routine performs no OAM writes.
The special attack box is a fixed $1C by $1E around its own position. Against primary colliders it only sets bits 4 and 7 of $22 and deals no damage at all.
The first loop always runs to completion before the damaging one starts.
Entered both after the primary loop and directly when the primary list is empty.
The bit test is followed by bne and then beq on the same flags, so the pair is an unconditional two-way branch and no path falls through to the loop tail.
Both damage paths return here rather than to a per-slot tail, because the special attack is a single object and may hit every target in the list on one frame.
An empty slot, an empty flag byte and an empty target list share this return.
The same bit-4 test and the same zero-health guard as the weapon path, so both damage routes agree on what a boss target is.
Unlike the weapon path it merges the attacker $21 byte into CombatHitFlags and into the target $22, and it never sets the weapon $26 to $FFFF, so the special attack is not spent by a hit.
It marks the target with bit 4 before testing the armour bit, so even a blocked target is flagged as touched.
The same bit-7 suppression of the destroyed-enemy tally the weapon path uses.
The routine walks the player weapon list against the collision target list, testing a fixed sixteen-pixel box around each weapon against each target's own four stored bounds at $30 through $36.
Each weapon's box is rebuilt once per weapon rather than per target, so the inner loop only compares.
Bit 4 of the target's collision byte selects between the boss damage path and the ordinary one, which is the only thing that distinguishes them.
Every rejection and every completed hit converges here, so one weapon can damage several targets in the same pass.
An empty weapon list and an empty target list share this return.
A boss target is skipped entirely once BossHealth reaches zero, unless bit 2 of BossColorEffectFlags marks the defeat sequence as already running.

Boss damage is the weapon's own power multiplied by the target's multiplier at $24, subtracted from BossHealth and clamped at zero, and the same block clears the counter and maximum fields on the killing hit.
Ordinary targets subtract the weapon power directly from their own health at $24 and are skipped when that field is already negative.
Bit 7 of the target's flags suppresses the destroyed-enemy counter, and bit 6 makes the target also spend one unit of the separate special-target count.
The routine walks only the collision list selected by object flag bit 5.
Each entry dispatches one of three player-to-moving-platform contact handlers.
Each registered platform is dispatched individually, so a single frame can resolve contact with several.
An empty platform list returns here, and the platform handler table also names this label as its no-contact mode.
The dispatcher selects a contact handler using the object's mode field at offset 0x46.
The handlers place the player on a platform top or underside and are not limited to a ship.
Four words measured from Collision_PlayerLandOnPlatform: a no-op mode, landing on top, contact with the underside, and the clamping variant.
After bounds checks the routine places the player at object Y minus 0x20 and links horizontal displacement.
No ship-specific state or data is accessed.
A rising player and every failed bounds test share this return, so landing resolves only while descending.
The routine clamps the player to object Y minus 0x20 for either vertical travel direction.
It is selected from the generic platform handler table and contains no Z-Leo-specific reference.
A descending player is attached and carried by the platform's own horizontal delta, while a rising one is only clamped, which is what makes this variant different from the landing handler.
The four bounds tests and the already-above case share this return.
After overlap tests the routine places the player at object Y plus 0x20 and sets underside-contact flags.
It initializes neither a stage nor an enemy.
The underside handler accepts a stationary player as well as a rising one, which the zero test before it allows.
An inverted player skips the lower bound test entirely, so a ceiling-attached player latches onto the underside from a wider range.
A descending player and every failed bounds test share this return.
The routine stages packed-BCD 0001 and adds it with two ABCD instructions to DestroyedEnemyCountBCD.
Carry saturates the displayed destroyed-enemy count at 9999; no subtraction occurs.

Once the animation counter passes $80 the object hides itself with $1000 into the sprite word, the bit-4 hide flag; until then a separate $48 counter only clears the collision byte, so the object outlives its own hitbox.
The collision byte is cleared once and the countdown then runs negative harmlessly.
The visibility countdown returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; after it becomes negative, the path clears byte $21 first.
It falls straight through into the slot search when the shared ExplosionSoundDelay is still positive, and re-arms the delay to $FFFF otherwise.

It finds a free slot, selects one of two impact-frame tables and clears d0 so the caller sees Z set; it spawns nothing itself. Boss_SniperHoneyviperSpawnDebris shows the contract: jsr, bne to skip, then Sprite_InitType58FromTable with a0 and a1 already loaded. The former Update name claimed work it does not do.
The sound fires on every $20th frame, and on one frame in eight of the rest when bit 3 of the random state is set, so the explosion crackle is irregular rather than periodic.

The routine ends here: it finds a free slot, picks a frame table and clears d0 so the caller sees Z set. It spawns nothing itself. Boss_SniperHoneyviperSpawnDebris shows the contract exactly: jsr, bne to skip, then Sprite_InitType58FromTable with a0 and a1 already loaded.
One draw in four on bits 8 and 9 of the random state takes the weapon impact frames instead of the general spawn frames.
A full object pool returns here with Z clear, which is what the callers test.
The same delay guard as its neighbour, but on the boundary frame it only plays a sound and returns; only while the delay is still running does it enter the slot search.
The same irregular sound cadence, here as a tail jump into the sound queue.
The silent boundary frames return here, and with them the caller sees the flags left by the last test rather than a slot result.
It raises both plane shake levels to 4, the highest this module uses, against the 2 the generic shake helper sets.
Four projectiles at $20 units of angle apart starting from $150, with the vertical component doubled and the horizontal shifted left five, so the spread is a flattened cross.
The sine and cosine are read $80 bytes apart in the same table, the idiom every spawner in this codebase uses for a direction pair.
A full pool ends the loop early, so fewer than four may appear.
Type $A8 with the sprite word cleared outright, which is unusual: every other initialiser here writes a non-zero attribute word.
Two instructions that set both plane shake levels to 2, the value most callers want.
Two nested counters: $48 paces the spawns two frames apart and $4A counts how many remain, and the object hides itself when $4A runs out but still spawns on that frame.
The jitter is a random $F on each axis, negated independently by two more random bits, so the particles fill a box rather than a line.
The vertical half of the same two-bit sign choice.
The routine ends by tail-jumping into RandomNumber, so the next spawn uses a fresh state.
Both the paced frames and a full pool return here.
Type $180. It writes d0 into $48 and then immediately clears $48, so the first store has no effect.
Gravity $3000 a frame, and a child spawned every two frames with an upward $11000, so the trail rises against the parent falling.
Both the paced frames and a full pool return here.
It retypes the current object first and then spawns four children, so the caller becomes part of the burst.
Each child takes its velocity pair from consecutive words of the table below, so the four fly out along the diagonals.
A full pool ends the loop early.
Eight words read as four pairs, each component plus or minus one, so the four directions are the corners of a unit square.
A one-instruction entry that points a0 at the current object and falls into the general initialiser below.
The shared table reader: four words into $4C, $E, 8 and $A, then the remaining table address into $48 as the animation script pointer.
The first of eight thin wrappers that differ only in the type word they write; this half of the family takes the current object.
The a0 half of the same pair, and the one Projectile_PrepareImpactSpawn callers use.
Type $68 from the current object.
Type $68 from a0.
Type $94 from the current object.
Type $94 from a0. Its only caller is Orphaned_SpawnType94RandomAngle, so this wrapper is live only through a dead one.
Type $A4 from the current object, and the target of the two orphaned thunks in weapons/projectile_impacts.s.
The routine calls the table initializer for the object already supplied in a0 and then writes type A4.
It performs no pool scan or free-slot test.
It masks the palette bits out of the sprite attribute and reinstalls one of two values by bit 1 of the frame counter, so the object alternates palette lines every two frames.
The alternate line is $6000 against $4000.
The routine advances the current animation frame and merges global stage bits into sprite attributes.
It neither consumes an initialization table nor allocates a projectile.

It subtracts $10000 and falls straight into the routine that adds $8000, so the net effect of this entry is $8000 upward and the entry below it is $8000 downward. One pair of instructions serves both directions.
The routine adds 0x8000 to the vertical velocity field.
The engine's paired entry point subtracts velocity for upward acceleration before falling through here.
The script format is a word count followed by three attribute words, and a negative count ends it. The pointer lives in $48 and is advanced in place.
The frames inside one script step return here.
This branch is reached only when the animation script reads a negative end marker.
It writes the hidden display state and contains no boss-specific behavior.
The routine reads generic frame records through the pointer stored at object offset 0x54.
At the end marker it restores velocities and jumps through the callback stored at offset 0x48.

The end marker in this variant is a jump: the script pointer in $48 is treated as code and entered, with $4C and $50 copied into the velocity fields first, so a script can hand control to a routine when it finishes.
The same script walker as Anim_UpdateSpriteFrame with a different end action and a different pointer field.
The frames inside one step return here.
It hides by clearing bit 15 of the sprite word rather than setting bit 4, so this module contains both of the two hide mechanisms this audit has pinned.
The looping variant reads a new script pointer out of the stream itself at the end marker, so a script can restart or chain to another.
The restart re-enters here rather than at the routine head, which is what skips the counter test on the wrap frame.
The frames inside one step return here.
The long following the end marker is the next script address.
The entry copies a5 to a0 and falls directly into the type-88 projectile initializer.
Its callers therefore initialize the current object rather than merely retrieving an address.
Type $88, then the shared effect graphics tail.
The entry copies a5 to a0 and falls into code that writes object type 188 and shared effect graphics.
No seeking-missile address is stored or returned separately.
Type $188, the same shape one type apart.
The entry copies a5 to a0 and falls through to the type-1A8 initializer.
Its observable behavior is projectile initialization, not a register-copy wrapper.
The first write assigns object type 0x1A8.
The value 0x2A does not occur in the routine.
Type $1AC, and the only one of the family that points a0 at the current object itself rather than having a separate entry for it.
The entry copies a5 to a0 and falls through to code that writes object type 160 and graphics attributes.
It initializes the current object rather than storing an object pointer.
Type $160, and the last of the family to fall into the shared tail.
The shared tail writes sprite word $ED40 and attribute $480 and clears the collision byte, so every effect type in the family starts inert.
Gravity $2000 a frame and then the height check below, which the handler table also names separately.
Both this label and the routine above it are named by Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, so an object can take the height check without the gravity.
Physics_CheckHeightBoundary branches to this RTS when $C(a5) compares below $80; the other path writes $1000 to sprite field 2 before the same return.
Two instructions and a hide, the simplest handler in the file.
The delayed-hide helper returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; a negative result writes object flags $1000 first.
Gravity $3000, and again the label below it is a separate handler-table entry so the motion can be had without the acceleration.
It applies the global flip bits and then the slot-based priority alternation before the height check.
Projectile_FallWithGravity_Update applies global attributes and slot priority, then branches to this RTS when $C(a5) compares below $80; the other path sets sprite field 2 to $1000.
The routine masks and merges word FF8092 into the sprite attribute field at offset 0x0E.
It reads neither an angle nor either velocity field.
The routine tests the object's RAM-slot bit and frame parity, then sets or clears bit 7 of display state.
It performs no trigonometry and never accesses a velocity field.

Bit 5 of the slot address and bit 0 of the frame counter are combined so that half the pool renders in front on even frames and the other half on odd. It is the fourth use of that address bit this audit has found, after the beam sound, the particle child spawn and the seeking missile re-aim.
The mirrored half of the same exclusive-or.
The clearing half.
The entry copies a5 to a0 and falls into debris initialization with randomized velocity.
Its effect extends beyond register forwarding.

The horizontal velocity is the whole random word sign-extended and shifted left three, so it spans both directions, while the vertical is only a two-bit negative, so debris always drifts upward slightly.
Gravity $4000, the strongest of the three falling handlers in this file.
Projectile_FallingDebris adds $4000 to vertical velocity, then branches to this RTS when $C(a5) compares below $80; the other path sets sprite field 2 to $1000.
It hides itself first and then sweeps the whole object pool up to $DCA0, clearing every object of type $12C or $134 that does not have bit 1 of its sprite word set.
Two types are matched against one scan, which is why both are named in the routine.
Bit 1 of the sprite word exempts an object from the sweep.
The stride is $60 and the limit is the absolute address $DCA0 rather than a count.
The routine loads object graphics metadata and writes a terminated pattern into the terrain tile map.
It contains no visibility test and never clears or destroys the object.
Index 7 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, which is type $1C. It is the shared behaviour machine several enemies use, and its variations come from the feature bits in $5F rather than from separate code.
A $5A field below $FF00 converts the object outright, and otherwise the field is spent as a lifetime counter that installs animation $13 when it runs out.
The random state is advanced once per object per frame, which is what gives the movement timers below their spread.
State then animation, the same two-step shape every controller in this audit uses.
Six self-relative words measured from Enemy_MainStateMachine rather than from the table, so an absolute-address scan finds none of the six handlers.
Six entries, and four of them name labels inside Enemy_MainStateMachine rather than separate routines, so the state machine is one routine entered at six different points.

State 0 sets up the sprite and falls into the move selector. The bits of $5F are the whole enemy variation: bit 0 skips the idle pause, bit 1 leaps at a wall instead of turning, bit 2 allows the ranged attack, bit 3 leaps when the player is within $50, and bit 4 suppresses facing the player.
The idle timer is a random $3F plus 8, so between 8 and $47 frames, and bit 0 of $5F skips it entirely.
State 2. Losing floor contact at any point diverts to the airborne entry, which is true of three of the six states.
Two distance thresholds: inside $78 with bit 2 set the enemy starts its attack cooldown, and inside $50 with bit 3 set it leaps.
The nearer test is second, so an enemy with both bits set attacks rather than leaps when it is between $50 and $78.
The frames that reach neither threshold return here.
Bit 4 of $5F skips the facing update. The branch after it is bra.w *+4, which targets the instruction immediately following, so it is a four-byte no-op left in the code.
The movement timer is a random $7F plus $80, between $80 and $FF frames, which is roughly four times the idle one.
State 4, and also the fall-through from the movement setup. Bit 0 of $5F makes it skip its own timer and run movement unconditionally.
The wall test is selected by the facing bit: bit 1 of 7(a5) when facing right and bit 0 when facing left.
The left-facing half of the same wall test.
With bit 1 of $5F the enemy leaps at the wall instead of turning; otherwise it flips the sprite flip bit and zeroes its velocity.
Both the wall-free and the turned case converge on the acceleration and then re-enter the distance checks.
Losing the floor halves the horizontal velocity and installs a small upward $12000, so an enemy that walks off a ledge drifts rather than dropping.
The leap is a much larger $58000 upward with $18000 horizontal, oriented by the facing.
Both airborne entries share state 6 and animation $14.
State 6. The sign of the gravity result selects the rising or the descending probe, the same split the player terrain code uses.
A rising enemy tail-jumps into the upper probe, so it cannot land on the same frame it is checked for a ceiling.
Landing arms a $14-frame grounded pause with animation $C.
State 8. Like the other grounded states it decelerates and diverts to the airborne entry the moment floor contact is lost.
The attack window is $36 frames with animation $10.
State $A. The shot is fired on the single frame the counter equals $1E, and from $10 frames down the enemy stops turning to face the player.
The facing update runs only while more than $10 frames remain, so the enemy commits to its aim before the shot.
Index $AC of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, which is type $2B0. Its two states are the destruction delay, so the former AnimationWrapper name described the tail call rather than the object.
The routine indexes a two-entry handler table using the object's state field and jumps to the selected handler.
It does not read coordinates or compare screen bounds.
Two self-relative words measured from Enemy_BeginDestructionDelay.
The routine initializes a fixed 0x24-frame destruction delay and then falls into its updater.
It performs no offscreen test.
This state decrements the existing delay and converts the object to its terminal effect type at expiry.
The destruction state was initialized by the preceding entry point; this code is its updater.
The routine derives a muzzle position from direction-indexed offsets and the current object coordinates.
It dispatches through a table containing the beam, bullet, homing, spread, and circular weapon handlers.
It does not construct sprite pieces or write the sprite output buffer.

Weapon_UpdatePlayerFiring reads the signed X byte at (a4,d6.w) and the signed Y byte eight bytes later. Its btst #3,$E(a5) followed by beq skips neg.w d1 when the bit is clear, so X is negated only when bit 3 is set; Y is never negated in this routine.
The routine uses the current weapon index to select one entry from the adjacent fire-handler table.
It performs an indirect jump and contains no ammo or effect-visibility test.

Eleven self-relative words measured from Weapon_DirectionIndexTable, not from the table itself, which is why a scan for absolute handler addresses finds nothing. Six distinct handlers: the last four slots and the first all resolve to Weapon_FireNoOp.
Eight identity bytes, 0 to 7, indexed by the aim index in $9E. It is also the base the handler offsets are measured from, so the same label serves as data and as a dispatch anchor.
Weapon type 1. An empty magazine diverts to Effect_SpawnRandomDebris rather than returning, so a dry weapon still produces its visual. The cooldown is two frames.
Eight slots of SharedEffectObjectPool at a $60 stride, scanned from the front, so the lowest free slot always wins.
Both a running cooldown and a full pool return here.
The three palette registers are the muzzle flash. In fixed-shooting mode an extra two units are charged before the difficulty cost below, so moving-shooting mode is cheaper by exactly that.
The test is tst.b on DifficultyMode, a byte read of the always-zero high half of a word variable, so the branch is never taken and the cost is always 1 rather than the 2 the code appears to charge.
The magazine is clamped at zero rather than wrapping.
The projectile carries two function pointers, an initialiser in $48 and a frame list in $54, so the object pipeline rather than this routine builds its sprite.

The damage test two instructions above this label is tst.w on the same variable and does work: difficulty 0 gives 4 and any other difficulty 3. The same routine therefore contains one difficulty test that functions and one that cannot, distinguished only by the operand size.

Installed as the $48 initialiser above and reached through the object pipeline, which is why it takes a5 rather than a0. The three parallel tables below are indexed by the direction octant left in $5C.
Eight words, one per direction octant, and the knockback particle effect reads the same table.
The parallel size table, indexed by the same octant; the four diagonal entries all share $A00.
The third parallel table, holding signed byte pairs, with the diagonals again sharing one value.
It jitters the muzzle position by plus or minus 8 on both axes from two separate bytes of the random state before placing the object, so the homing shots do not stack.
The same eight-slot forward scan the other handlers use.
Only the cooldown reaches this return; a full pool returns from inside the scan.
Unlike the ordinary projectile it writes the velocity pair straight into $18 and $1C rather than into the $4C and $50 scratch pair, so it moves under the generic object physics.
The companion comes from PlayerEffectObjectPool and only three slots are scanned, against eight for the shot itself.
The companion inherits both velocities divided by four, so the trail drifts at a quarter of the shot speed.
Three interleaved eight-word rows in one block: tiles at offset 0, sizes at $10 and offsets at $20, all indexed by the same octant. Weapon_HandleProjectileHit reads the same block.
Weapon type 2. It counts the free slots first and stores their addresses into SharedSpriteScratch, then fires only if at least four are available, so a partly full pool produces nothing at all.
The scan records every free slot, not just the first four, and d3 ends as the total count.
Both a taken and a free slot converge on the pointer step.

Zero incoming references: the only two source mentions are its own definition and the outgoing cross-reference comment on Weapon_InitSpreadShot, and the routine above it ends in rts so it cannot be fallen into. The single ROM address match, at $43A20 inside Boss_ViblackInit, is a false positive: those bytes are the $0001 immediate and the $8218 short address of move.w #1,(PaletteEffectControl).w, not a pointer. It would charge a flat $12 of ammo with no difficulty test before falling into the live spread initialiser.

Its damage test is tst.w and works: 2 at difficulty 0 and 1 otherwise. It also nudges the spawn position two steps along the aim vector and gives the object the negated vector divided by eight as its drift.
The horizontal component has the stage scroll delta multiplied by four added to it, so spread shots inherit the scrolling of the stage and the plain projectile does the same.
Shared by the spread initialiser and by both early exits of Weapon_FireMultipleShots.
Reached only when four or more slots are free. Its flash level is $E0 against the $80 of the single shot.
Another tst.b site, so the cost is always $12 and never the $14 the code appears to charge on higher difficulties.
The four-shot spread subtracts D0 from ammo at $10(a4), where D0 is $12 on zero difficulty and $14 otherwise; negative results are clamped to zero before the four-projectile spawn loop.
The direction index is pre-decremented by $14 so that the first pass of the loop, which adds 8, lands on the intended first octant.
Four shots at 8 units of direction apart, masked to $7C, so the spread covers a quarter turn and wraps within the vector table.
The routine writes the object type, display state, and two object-state bytes.
It neither advances an animation nor assigns an animation frame table.

At $018326 this label contains only RTS. No direct source reference or 32-bit ROM occurrence of its absolute address was found, so it is orphaned in the current static evidence; a computed indirect call is not excluded.
Weapon type 3. It is the only handler that checks bit 7 of PlayerRestrictionFlags, and it has no cooldown of its own; the rate is set by the firing code that calls it.
The same eight-slot forward scan.
The fixed-shooting surcharge is two units here as well.
A third tst.b site: the cost is always 3 and never 4.
The bullet handler subtracts D0 from ammo at $10(a4), where D0 is 3 on zero difficulty and 4 otherwise; negative results are clamped to zero before object setup.
Object type $18 with no initialiser pointer, so this handler builds its own object rather than deferring to the pipeline.

Its damage test is tst.w and works, 4 at difficulty 0 and 3 otherwise. The velocity vectors come from a table whose address is read out of WeaponModeParameter, so this weapon can be retargeted at run time.
The sound plays on one frame in four, gated by the frame counter, and the other three return here.
A bare return with zero references of any kind, no ROM absolute-address match, and preceded by a return, so it is unreachable on every path. Its address comes from build/main.lst.
Weapon type 4. Its cooldown is a single frame, the shortest of the four, which is what makes it the continuous one.
The same eight-slot forward scan.
Both the cooldown and a full pool return here.
The fixed-shooting surcharge is four units here, twice that of the other handlers.
The fourth and last tst.b site in this module: the cost is always 1 and never 2.
The beam handler subtracts D0 from ammo at $10(a4), where D0 is 1 on zero difficulty and 2 otherwise; negative results are clamped to zero before beam-object setup.
Its damage test is tst.w and works, 2 at difficulty 0 and 1 otherwise, so all four handlers pair a working damage test with a dead ammo test.

The aim byte is jittered by a random entry of the offset table and stored in $57, and the firing sound is gated on bit 5 of the slot address, so only half the pool positions make a noise. The skip branches to Weapon_FireNoOp, using the shared no-op as a return.

Live and heavily shared: five slots of the handler table name it, the beam data routine branches to it as a return, and Player_SpawnCircleAttack uses it the same way. Its address comes from build/main.lst.
Eight bytes stepping by $10, which convert the aim index into a byte offset into the direction vector tables. Three handlers and the homing spawner all index through it.
Eight signed bytes, $FC $F8 $FC 0 0 4 8 4, drawn by three random bits, so the beam aim wanders by at most two steps either way and is unjittered on two of the eight draws.

Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, and the bytes before it are the jitter table, so nothing can fall into it. It would build a type-$A0 companion at a fixed $300 bytes above the beam object and seed its $4C from bit 5 of that address, the same bit the live beam code uses to halve its sound rate.
The third of the three empty companion handlers, all unreferenced, all immediately after the routine they would have accompanied. Its address comes from build/main.lst.

Weapon_FireHandlerOffsets names this handler by a word offset from Weapon_DirectionIndexTable, not by an absolute address. It needs all eight shared effect slots free at once, so a single leftover object cancels the whole attack.
The scan aborts on the first occupied slot rather than counting free ones, which is what makes the all-or-nothing requirement.
Both arms of this difficulty test load the same $8C, so the cost is fixed even before the byte-test problem below applies.
The subtraction clamps at zero rather than wrapping, so firing with insufficient ammo is allowed and simply empties the gauge.
The aim index selects a sine and cosine pair scaled by $27 as the shared orbit offset, and the player-to-target delta is cached once for all eight projectiles.
All eight projectiles share one velocity and one orbit offset and differ only in the phase stored in $5E, which advances by three per slot.
Each projectile takes the player's draw bucket minus four so it renders in front, and the lifetime is $D or $E depending on difficulty, which here is a genuine word test.
An occupied slot returns here with the cooldown already spent.
Four long pointers over three distinct frame sets; the second and fourth entries are the same, which mirrors the diagonal cases.
Three eight-word rows, indexed together by the rounded aim: sprite attribute words, size words and the signed display offset pairs.

A bare return with no caller, no absolute address in the ROM, and no entry in Weapon_FireHandlerOffsets, while the two live handlers in this module both resolve in that table. Its former name claimed a companion-handler role nothing supports.
The other handler this module contributes to the weapon table. It fires on alternate frames only and, unlike the circle attack, takes the first free slot instead of requiring all eight.
The scan stops at the first free slot, which is the opposite convention to the circle attack's.
The off-frame case and a full effect pool share this return.
Moving-shooting mode costs an extra two units of ammo before the per-difficulty cost is applied.

The test is tst.b on DifficultyMode, a word variable at $FFFFFF0E whose value never exceeds two, so the byte read is the always-zero high half and the branch is never taken. The cost is therefore always the lower value, 2 rather than 3.
The same clamp-at-zero behaviour as the circle attack.
The shot stores its spawn point and the player-relative target delta, and its lifetime is 3 or 4 by a genuine word test on the same variable.
The velocity pair comes from the table WeaponModeParameter points at, indexed by the aim, so the equipped weapon mode selects the speed profile rather than the code.
The firing sound plays on only half the shots, gated on a second frame-counter bit.
The same three-row layout as the circle attack's table, with its own attribute, size and offset values.
The second unreferenced bare return in this module, checked the same way as the first.

Unreferenced, absent from the ROM as an absolute address, and absent from the weapon handler table. It would read a signed offset pair from a table at a4, mirror the horizontal half by facing, and place an object relative to the player.
The right-facing half of that unreferenced pair, which skips the negation.
Both the plain and the multi-shot fire handlers divert here when the weapon gauge is empty, so this is what an out-of-ammo trigger produces instead of a shot.
The debris uses the same eight-slot shared effect pool the two weapons compete for.
The off-frame case and a full pool share this return.
Each particle takes a randomized position offset and velocity and plays its own sound.
The completed particle returns here.
The routine tests one object-state flag and compares the animation counter at offset 0x0C with 0x80.
Either terminal condition sets the same inactive-object bit used by the surrounding removal handlers.
It does not read a health or damage field and contains no enemy-specific reference.
Both the explicit flag and an animation frame counter past $80 converge on the same removal bit.
An object still inside its animation returns here unchanged.
Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs this handler, and it is found by the absolute-address scan, which is what distinguishes it from the weapon-table handlers in the same module.
The marker object is shown on alternate frames and follows the sight, so the selected slot blinks.
A sight that is not the currently selected slot returns without touching the marker.
A single instruction shared by both exits of the rotating-projectile update.
The object dispatch table invokes this routine as a recurring update handler.
Its state flags select initial motion, lifetime countdown, or impact initialization for the existing object.
It does not allocate a new object slot.
The particle takes a fully random direction at a fixed speed shift of four and installs its own sprite table.
On expiry the particle halves both velocity components and switches to the impact frames rather than disappearing.
Frames inside the lifetime return here.
The impact variant installs its own tile source and attribute word before entering the shared motion below.
Two projectile-impact handlers also enter here; the block picks a random direction from the speed-10 vector table, halves it, and plays SFX $C8.

It steps a four-bit frame index and reads three parallel words from a table whose address is in $4A, then culls itself outside the box $80 to $1C0 by $A0 to $160. Gravity is suppressed entirely while bit 0 of PlayerModeFlags is set.
The suppressed-gravity frames return here.

Three collision bits are consumed with bclr in one chain, so each is tested and cleared in the same instruction: bit 7 of $22 is the hit, bit 6 of $23 the terrain contact and bit 4 of $23 the armour block.
The impact path stops the projectile dead and hands it to the shared type-A4 initialiser with the impact frame table.
The burst path installs Weapon_HomingEffectSpriteData, the same block weapons/firing.s builds its homing shots from, and tail-branches into the shared impact motion.

A one-instruction thunk to Sprite_InitTypeA4FromCurrentTable with no reference of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match. The routine above it ends in the very same jmp, inline, so the thunk reads as a helper that was inlined and left behind.
Shared by the hit handler and reached only when neither the terrain nor the armour bit was set, so a projectile that touches nothing simply ages.
The same three-bclr chain as the ordinary hit handler, differing only in where the no-contact case goes: here it animates a fade rather than ticking a lifetime.

A zero WeaponModeParameter skips the explosion entirely and takes the plain impact instead. Otherwise the velocity is divided by eight and the object is retyped to $400 with five or six points of damage.
The damage test here is tst.w on DifficultyMode and works: 6 at difficulty 0 and 5 otherwise, matching the pattern that every damage test in the weapon code is a word read.
Identical to the impact path of the ordinary handler, including the same frame table.
Identical to the burst path of the ordinary handler, instruction for instruction.
A second thunk to Sprite_InitTypeA4FromCurrentTable, also unreferenced and also immediately after a routine that performs the same jmp inline.
The fade counter in $5E is spent two at a time and shifted right two, so the four table entries each cover eight counter steps.
The index is clamped to 6 and masked to 6, so the last entry is held rather than the table being walked past its end.
Four tiles, the last of which is the single-tile $45A0.
The parallel sizes, ending at zero, which is a one-tile sprite.
The parallel offsets, shrinking from $F4F4 to $FCFC as the sprite gets smaller, so the explosion stays centred as it fades.
The routine only sets bit 4 of the object display-state word.
The same write terminates objects throughout the adjacent projectile and effect handlers; no priority field is calculated.
It drives the palette flash registers directly and then hides the effect once its animation counter passes $80, writing $1000 into the sprite word rather than freeing the slot.
The only comparison uses the animation counter at object offset 0x0C and the terminal value 0x80.
At the terminal frame it replaces the display-state word with the hidden state 0x1000.
No damage or health field is read.
The frames before the animation ends return here.
State flags choose between updating the current particle animation and attempting to allocate a child effect.
Both paths finish by marking the current object inactive, so spawning is only one state of the handler.

Only half the pool spawns a child: bit 5 of the slot address decides, and the other half deactivates at once. It is the same address-bit halving the beam firing sound and the seeking missile both use.
The child takes one of two frame tables chosen by bit 7 of the random state, so the particle shape is a coin flip.
The direction is the parent angle in $56 rounded by adding $20 and masked to $7C, so the eight sectors are centred rather than started on.
Bit 1 of the frame counter negates the whole vector, so successive particles fly in opposite directions, and the result is quartered before the shared motion parameters are added.
Reached from both refusals and from the end of the spawn, and it sets bit 4 of the sprite flag byte, the hide flag this audit has pinned across four modules.
The animation path spends $48 two at a time and uses it directly as a word index into three parallel eight-entry tables.
Eight tiles whose first five repeat a three-value cycle, so the particle pulses before it shrinks.
The parallel sizes, stepping down $F00, $A00, $500 across the last three entries.
The parallel offsets, stepping in to match.

The missile re-aims only on half the frames for half the slots: the frame counter parity and bit 5 of the slot address together mean each missile runs its arctangent on alternate frames, which halves the cost across the pool.
The impact path arms three frames of the shared animation 12 and stops the missile.
A missile whose lifetime passes $FFF1 hides itself with bit 4 of the sprite flag byte, the hide flag this audit has pinned across four modules, so it has $10 frames of grace after expiry.
The two bit tests are what split the pool into the two halves that re-aim on alternate frames.
The mirrored half of the same split.
With no target recorded in WeaponTargetOrFrame the heading is taken straight from the random state, so an untargeted missile wanders.
Bit 0 of the target word is cleared before it is used as a slot address, which is the same one-bit flag packing the Jetsripper direction table uses.
The turn rate is a random 6 to $C per step, so two missiles launched together diverge.
The increasing half of the shortest-arc turn.
The wrap test at $FFC0 is what makes the turn take the short way round.
The decreasing half.

The velocity table address is read out of WeaponModeParameter and the result is shifted by a count read out of WeaponXMotionParameter+2, so both the vector set and the speed scale are set by the caller.
The frame index is forced to 4 once the lifetime goes negative, so an expiring missile freezes on one frame.
The smaller sprite is used for the first two indices only; the selection is by frame index, not by distance as the former comment claimed.
Eight tiles over five distinct values, with $45AD appearing three times.
The parent is found by subtracting a fixed $300 or $360 from the companion slot address, alternating by frame parity, which is the same $300 stride Weapon_InitProjectileCompanion adds.
The alternate stride is $360, one object further back.
The companion checks that the parent still holds the same value in $48 before copying, and parks itself at X $40 when it does not.
The copied position is the parent position minus its velocity, so the companion renders where the parent was on the previous frame.
The $5E counter arms the collision byte on the exact frame it reaches zero, so the projectile is harmless for its first frames.
The motion is a subtraction rather than an addition, so $48 and $4C hold the negated velocity.
Named by Entity_UpdateHandlerTable in its own right as well as being the collision path of the routine above it.
A projectile with health remaining returns here untouched.
The sound plays only when the armour bit is also set, so a clean hit is silent.
Both the loud and the silent case converge on the explosion spawn.
The companion is at a fixed $300 bytes above the projectile, the same stride the companion updater subtracts.
The velocity is a sine and a cosine, taken $80 bytes apart in the same table, each shifted left by three or four from a random bit, so both magnitude and direction are randomised.
It is the only projectile in the module that positions itself relative to the player rather than in world coordinates.
On expiry it hides itself, clears its collision byte, and hands its position and a quarter of its velocity to the companion $300 bytes above.
The position is PlayerXPosition plus a fixed offset in $58 plus an accumulator in $50, and the same again vertically, so the bomb drifts in the player frame of reference.
The same silent-or-loud split the seeking projectile uses, with the same SFX $C8.
The debris spawn and the companion update are both done here, so an exploding bomb produces two objects.
Instruction for instruction Effect_SpawnExplosion with the shift seeds two lower, so the debris flies at a quarter of the explosion speed.
Sixteen slots are scanned, twice the eight the weapon handlers use, and the spark is type $7C.
A full pool simply returns, so a death spark can be dropped.
The initial velocity is a cosine scaled by $20 and a sine indexed by the frame counter shifted left five, and both are also stored unscaled into $4E and $50 for the deceleration below.
The spark hides itself with bit 4 of the sprite flag byte, the hide flag this audit has pinned across four modules once its animation counter passes $80.
The deceleration subtracts the stored initial components once per frame, so the spark decays along its own launch axis rather than toward zero.
Two instructions and a return: spend $48 and hide the object when it goes negative.
The removal countdown returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; a negative result sets object flag bit 4 first.
Bit 7 of the sprite word is set only while the player mapping is the teleport dash trail, so the effect follows a specific player state.
Twelve slots are scanned and a hit on bit 7 of $22 also arms a four-frame freeze, the same hit-stop the collision code uses.
The vertical offset is a cosine indexed by the frame counter shifted left five, negated on alternate frames, so successive sparks alternate above and below.
The horizontal speed is $A0000 rightward against $FFF60000 leftward, chosen by the sign of PlayerStateWorkHighWord.
A full pool returns here.
It advances $1C, which for this object is an animation counter rather than a velocity, and hides the object when $48 runs out.
The animation/lifetime helper increments frame field $1C and returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; expiry sets object flag bit 4.
The entry fixes a0 to the shared object-pool base and d7 to 0x10 before entering the common clearing loop.
The common loop clears exactly 96 bytes per DBF iteration, so this entry clears 17 object-sized blocks rather than an arbitrary memory block.
Each loop iteration contains 24 longword stores and therefore clears one 96-byte object block.
The three adjacent entry points supply the shared object-pool base and counts of 8, 16, or 17 blocks.

Zero references of any kind: no caller anywhere in the source, no ROM absolute-address match, and Stage_StopScrollEffect above it ends in rts so it cannot be fallen into. Everything below it is reachable only through this routine, so the whole wave state machine is dead.

Six absolute long pointers, which is why the reachability scan reports a ROM hit for each handler at this table rather than at a call site. Reached only from the orphaned controller. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.

State 0. It runs the parameter index from 0 up to $1C in steps of two, then hands over with a $78-frame timer. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The frames before the index reaches $1C return here.

State 1 holds the deformation at full strength for $78 frames and reads its wave data from $FFFF9E40, the same base the init state uses. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The wave hold returns here while WaveStateTimer is nonzero after decrement; zero advances WaveStateOffset by four and reloads timer one.

State 2 runs the index back down from $1C to 6, not to zero, and reads from $FFFF9E80, a base used by no other state. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The frames before the index reaches 6 return here.

State 3 runs the index up from 6 to $1C again and then either repeats by stepping the state offset back four or advances, so states 2 and 3 form the repeating body of the effect. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The repeat path subtracts four from the state offset, returning to the fade-out state.
The frames inside the ramp return here.

State 4, the final wind-down: it takes the index from $1C down to zero and then advances into the empty state. It touches no camera field at all, so the former Camera_UpdateAndRenderStageTilemapEffect name was wrong on both halves. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The wave wind-down returns here while WaveParameterIndex remains nonzero after subtracting two; zero advances WaveStateOffset by four.
State 5, a bare return, and the state the wind-down advances into, so the machine parks here. It is referenced by the table rather than orphaned. Its address comes from build/main.lst.

A second bare return two bytes after the first, with no reference of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match. The rts above it means it cannot be fallen into either. Its address comes from build/main.lst.
The routine always fixes its destination to the wave output buffer at FFFF9800.
Its DBF counter starts at 0x50, so it clears 81 longwords rather than the 80 claimed by the generated comment.
It clears $51 long words, which is $144 bytes, of WaveOutputBuffer.
The sine table is filled outward from its centre in both directions at once, one accumulator adding the step and the other subtracting it, so the two halves are mirror images by construction.
Four columns are filled, each starting $50 bytes further into the output buffer.
The run length is $1C minus the start offset plus $B, so the later the effect has progressed the shorter each column run becomes.
Fifteen words descending from $85B8 to $8040, read with the parameter index as a byte offset, so the fifteen entries cover indices 0 to $1C in steps of two exactly.
The companion fifteen words descending from $E0 to 0, so the last entry gives a zero step and a flat sine table.

Its only caller is UnreferencedWave_RenderTilemapToVRAM, which nothing references. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.

The accumulator is split into a low three-bit tile column and a high field masked to $FFF8, then recombined, which packs a row and a column into one word. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.

Both pointers are built into sega_tiles, so the deformation would have been applied to the SEGA logo tiles. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The odd case selects nibble offset 4 against 0 for the even one.
The address arithmetic keeps two bits of the coordinate and shifts the rest left three, which is the layout of a four-byte-wide tile row.
The second pointer repeats the same arithmetic and adds 8 to the nibble offset when the first coordinate was even.

Four absolute long pointers selected by the nibble offset the pointer builder left in d0, so the blend routine is chosen by pixel alignment. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.

Four handlers covering the four combinations of the two nibble offsets. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.

The first of the four: high nibble from the first source, low from the second, eight pixels per row and four rows. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The row stride is 4 bytes and the block stride $160, so the routine walks a tile column rather than a tile.

The second combination, shifting the first source into the high nibble. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The same eight-by-four walk with the shift applied.
The third combination, shifting both halves. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The same walk again.
The fourth and last combination. It is second-order dead code: referenced, and so not orphaned by the project rule, but its only route in is through a caller that nothing reaches.
The same walk, completing the four-way alignment set.
Live, unlike the wave machine above it: the tile loading half of this module is reached from the ending and teleport asset paths. It seeds the four parameter tables below.
The first of four parallel $1C-byte parameter tables, all read by the initialiser above.
The second parallel table.
The third parallel table.
The fourth parallel table, so the four together give fourteen words per parameter set.
Live: the init state and the wind-down state both call it, so it is an emptied hook rather than a cut routine. Its address comes from build/main.lst.
A binclude payload with no reference of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match. It sits between the parameter tables and the tile loader, and the existing name already records that it is unused.

Live. Two ROM absolute-address matches, inside EndingSequence_Initialize and Stage_LoadTeleportAssets, are genuine call sites rather than false positives, which is what separates this half of the module from the wave machine.
The step advances by the interpolation stride and the loop ends when the destination count runs out.
The interpolation is between two source tiles chosen by the current position, which is what makes the transition a morph rather than a cut.
It drives the interpolating decompressor once per tile pair.
The loop count comes from the caller rather than from a header.
It saves and restores the codec state around each pair, which is why the routine ends in a restore rather than a plain return.
The first source is selected by the high half of the position.
The position is clamped so the second source never runs past the last tile.
The second source is the tile after the first unless the clamp applied.
Thirty-two pixels per tile, processed as nibble pairs.
The first nibble is aligned by a shift chosen from the position parity.
The second nibble is aligned the same way with the opposite parity.
The saved codec state is restored here, which is what lets the caller keep decompressing after an interpolated pair.
It selects between a one, two, three or large block path by the tile count, so the loader has four unrolled shapes rather than one loop.
The two-block path.
The three-block path.
The large-block path, which is the only one that loops.
It clears the interpolation tile buffer before handing the asset list to the shared loader.
The destination is fixed to the 512-byte tile-interpolation workspace at FF9800.
Both callers immediately generate interpolated tile data into that workspace.

A two-byte thunk that is reached only by falling off the end of TransitionEffect_BuildSymmetricRamp_FillConstantLoop in the neighbouring module: that loop sits at $26C50 and its three instructions occupy exactly the eight bytes before this label. It is live, unlike the eight entry points around it.

Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, and the two-byte thunk before it ends in a branch so it cannot be fallen into. It would seed d5 with the RAM address $FFFF9B00 and enter the shared sine buffer builder.
The second entry point of the same dead pair, seeding d5 with the ROM sine table instead. It has no reference either, and the branch above it means no fall-through.
The shared body of the two dead entry points. Its only reference is the branch from the first of them, so the whole chain is unreachable.
A zero transition progress skips the reciprocal and leaves the step at zero, which would make every sample read the same table entry.
The step is a $8000 divided by the progress, doubled and shifted left eight, so the table is walked faster the earlier the transition is.
Each sample is written twice, backwards through a0 and forwards through a2 from the same buffer base, which builds a mirrored ramp in one pass.
Live: TransitionEffect_UpdateMode3Buffers calls it. The destination is the progress masked to $1FE and offset by -$6C00, so the write position moves with the transition rather than being fixed.
The repeat count is TransitionMaskStep, which the mode-3 handler clamps to zero if it has gone negative before calling this.

Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in rts. Its live counterparts Effect_ProcessConditionalScroll and Effect_ProcessSimpleScroll have the same shape and are both called from the mode handlers; this one and the horizontal variant below it are not.
The clamp range is 0 to $120, which is the only one of the four scroll processors to use that bound.
The low clamp forces zero.
The upper bound test against $120 is what separates this dead routine from the live $A0 one below it.
The centre adjustment is the step this routine has and the live simple processor does not.
Both the clamped and the adjusted value converge on this store.
Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, preceded by an rts. It is the $A0-bound twin of the dead vertical processor above it.
The doubled offset and the $FE mask are the same arithmetic the two live processors use.
Live: TransitionEffect_UpdateMode2Buffers calls it. The vertical half runs only while TransitionOriginXY is non-zero, which is what makes it conditional.
The vertical value is the sample quadrupled and subtracted from $140, and it is written twice so one entry covers two scanlines.
Both the skipped and the written vertical case converge on the index step.
Live: TransitionEffect_UpdateMode3Buffers branches to it. It writes the same constant vertical value for every line, which is the whole difference from the conditional processor above.
The constant comes from TransitionOriginXY and is written twice per iteration, matching the conditional processor pair for pair.

Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, preceded by an rts. It would modulate the linear base table by the quarter sine table with the phase advancing one step per scanline and wrapping at $FE.
The phase wraps within a byte, so the modulation repeats every $80 scanlines against the $80 lines the loop covers.
Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, preceded by an rts. It is the unmodulated twin of the routine above, reading the same base table with a plain accumulator.
The accumulator is the whole long at TransitionOriginXY, so the increment carries a fractional part.
Both AlternateTransition_Update and TransitionEffect_Update call it, and it writes no scroll value.
It loads PaletteActiveColor62 into a1 and stores one colour word at (a1) and at $80(a1), which is PaletteShadowColor62, so it drives palette entry 62 in both the active and the shadow buffer.
Every value it can store is a CRAM colour word: $EEE, $8CE, and the sixteen entries of Effect_TransitionColorRamp.
The common tail: it stores the chosen colour word into both palette buffers and returns.
It is reached while TransitionProgress is below $40, where the colour strobes between $EEE and $8CE on frame parity and a random bit, so the branch selects a colour rather than an initial pattern.

Once TransitionProgress reaches $40 the colour comes from Effect_TransitionColorRamp, indexed by the progress halved and masked to $1E, so the sixteen entries are walked once across the second half of the transition.
Sixteen CRAM colour words running from white ($EEE) through blue to near black (6), read only by Effect_UpdateTransitionColor62_SelectRampEntry.
It is a colour ramp, not a tile pattern: the genuine pattern data in this file lives in TransitionPatternBuffer, which this routine never touches.
Live: TransitionEffect_UpdateMode3Buffers calls it. It clears $40 long words, which is $100 bytes, of the pattern buffer.
A plain long-word clear.
A $100-byte binary payload read by both dead scroll appliers and by nothing else, so the table is as unreachable as they are.
The sine table the live edge generator and the live symmetric ramp builder both read, and also the dead sine buffer builder.
The routine reads transition tables and writes the FF9600, FF9800, FF9A00, and FF9B00 RAM workspaces.
It neither accesses the VDP ports nor writes palette RAM; later code consumes the generated buffers.
A zero progress leaves the step at zero, the same guard the dead builder has.
The step is TransitionEdgeSpan divided by the progress, so the edge sharpens as the transition advances.
Samples below the $FF00 threshold read the sine table; the rest are forced to zero, which is what gives the edge a flat outside.
The mirrored double store, backwards and forwards from one base, the same construct the dead builder uses.
The second loop turns the edge buffer into the two hardware scroll buffers, and its source pointer is pre-offset by the transition origin so the pattern slides.
Samples read from outside the $9A02 to $9C00 window are replaced by zero, which bounds the effect to the visible raster.
The difference between the origin and the sample selects between a gentle half-step adjustment and the clamped path.
The half step is applied and a negative result is zeroed.
Reached both from the adjust path and from the upper bound test below.
Bit 1 of the difference is carried into the vertical output, so the vertical scroll takes only a two-pixel granularity here.
The horizontal sample is clamped at $9E, four short of the $A2 the window allows.
A vertical value at or above $140 clears the sample entirely, and otherwise the sum of the sample and half the vertical is checked against $100.
The vertical is stored first and the horizontal is then reduced by the line index and masked, so the two buffers are filled in one pass.
The routine clears 24 longwords beginning at FF9400 and resets the transition progress counter.
It does not access either palette RAM or a palette data table.
It clears $18 long words, which is $60 bytes, against the $100 the other clear covers.
The routine writes a fixed arrangement of zero and 0xE nibble masks into the FF9400 pattern buffer.
It then queues the buffer-related VDP register setup but does not update a position or scroll accumulator.
Also the target of a branch from Orphaned_ScrollMaskPattern1, so this live label is entered from dead code as well as from its own routine.
Four iterations of two long words each, so the prefix is $20 bytes of the $EEEEEEEE fill.
Three iterations of two long words, so the suffix is $18 bytes of zero before the final pair.
