Live: AlternateTransition_BuildInitialPattern calls it. It lays down eight long words of fill, four of zero, four of fill and eight of zero, a different shape from Effect_BuildTransitionPattern.
The prefix is eight long words rather than the four pairs the other builder writes.
The suffix is eight long words of zero, and the routine then tail-branches into the shared register queue.

Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in a branch. What makes it unusual is that its tail is live: Effect_QueueTransitionVdpRegisters sits inside its body and is entered by four other routines, so the dead part is only the masking above that label.
The nibble mask is $F below step $20 and $F0 above it, so the mask would erase the two halves of a byte in two passes.

Live and shared by four routines. It pushes six VDP register writes onto the command queue head, growing the queue downwards, and the caller list is what keeps the dead masking routine above it assembled.
Sixteen words read as bytes by the dead masking routine, giving the pairs $00 $10, $01 $11 and so on, so the byte offsets walk two interleaved columns.
The routine selects two masks from a progress-indexed table and applies them to three rows of the transition pattern buffer.
It does not reset the object state or the transition progress value.
The routine loads the player object at FFA400 and returns the absolute horizontal delta in d0.
It returns the signed vertical delta in d2 and the constant 1 in d3; no norm, square, or root is calculated.
The optional negation converges here, so d0 holds the absolute horizontal distance while d2 keeps the signed vertical delta and d3 is set to one.

No caller references this routine and its absolute address does not occur in the ROM, while the control routines Sys_ClearEntityObjectPool and VDP_QueueCommand in the same region are both found by that scan. It subtracts the a1 object's coordinates from the a0 object's and scales the Math_Arctan2Lookup result into the $1FE angle range.

Boss_SniperHoneyviperLoadInitialAssetsAfterBackgroundRows and Boss_FlyingNeoInit call this builder, which fills three $200-byte quadrant buffers from the shared quarter-sine table scaled by d0, saving and restoring a5 through TrigSavedObjectPtr.
The 64-iteration loop writes each scaled quarter-sine entry forwards and backwards into the mirrored quadrant buffers, negating it for the two lower quadrants.
Sixty-five words rising from zero to $3FFB, one quadrant of a sine wave at $4000 scale; Math_LookupSineCosinePair and Projectile_SpawnType1A8AtAngle read it directly.
The full preserved sine table, included from its extracted binary segment.

Nothing calls this loop and its absolute address does not occur in the ROM. It walks $60-byte entity records up to $DCA0 and is a variant of the live Object_ClearEntityRecordsExceptTwoTypes at 0x1C288: that routine zeroes 61 records outright, while this one only marks each record for removal.
The per-record half of the same orphaned pair: it leaves a record alone when its type word is zero or matches either spared type in d0 and d1, and otherwise writes type $10 and removal flag $1000.
The three spared-record paths share this return.
The routine starts at Entity_ObjectPool and clears consecutive 96-byte records through address DCA0.
Frontend and cutscene callers use the same routine, so the storage is neither boss-specific nor a separate boss buffer.
The gameplay loop calls this entry, which does nothing while bit 7 of FrameControlFlags is set, spends one tick of StageSpawnCountdown while it is still positive, and then runs the spawn list.
A negative countdown is left alone, so the delay stops at -1 rather than wrapping.
Both delay paths converge on a PC-relative call into the spawn-list walker and then fall through into the visible-object pass.
The pass walks all 61 records of the entity pool, dispatching each live type through Entity_UpdateHandlerTable except type $10, which is updated elsewhere.
The loop body skips empty records outright and calls the handler indexed by the type word used directly as a table offset.
After the handler runs, bit 4 of the flags removes the object, and bit 1 selects whether it is culled by position at all.
An object outside X $60 to $1E0 or Y $40 to $170 is cleared rather than queued, which is the off-screen cull.
Surviving objects append their own record address to the visible-object list that the renderer consumes.
All three outcomes converge here to step one $60-byte record and stop at $DCA0, the end of the pool.
The walker does nothing while the cursor is negative or the camera is moving backwards, and otherwise spawns every record whose X lies within $140 pixels ahead of the camera.
Each accepted record advances the cursor by $C bytes, which is the twelve-byte stride of the spawn tables.
The first record beyond the lookahead window is written back as the new cursor, so the list is consumed strictly forwards.
The exhausted-cursor and backward-camera paths share this return.

One record supplies X and Y at offsets 0 and 2, the type and difficulty flags at 4, an extra word at 6 that becomes field $5E, and the slot range at 8 and $A. A free slot is preferred, and a reusable one is accepted only if no free slot exists.
Both slot searches converge here to clear the record before the difficulty flags are examined.
Bit 0 of the type word suppresses the object on the default difficulty and bit 1 suppresses it on the other, and both rejections return here with the slot already cleared.
The second flag is tested only when the first was clear, and both bits are removed from the word before it becomes the object type.
The accepted record writes the masked type, the extra word, and both coordinates, converting the stored X to a camera-relative position biased by $80 and the stored Y to a camera-absolute one.
A failed reusable-slot search returns here without touching the pool.
The scan looks for a zero type word between a5 and a0 and clears the zero flag explicitly when the range is exhausted, so the caller can distinguish the two outcomes.
A found slot returns here with the zero flag still set from the type test.
The routine scans 96-byte object records between bounds supplied by the caller and tests bit 6 of each record's state byte.
It returns a qualifying slot and status; it accesses neither palette data nor a VDP port.

Four callers reach this entry, whose first instruction is a branch to the next one and therefore a no-op; the block it falls into begins with a conditional branch, so the routine also depends on the allocation result its caller left in the flags.
The object is scattered inside a 32-pixel box centred on the caller and given one of four vertical velocities from the table below, with the upward pair also taking a negative secondary field.
A failed allocation and the two downward velocity cases share this return.
Four long velocities, two upward and two downward, selected by two bits of the random state; the index also decides the sign of the secondary field at $5C.
Sixteen boss defeat paths call this. It walks all 61 records and clears the collision byte of any object whose flags overlap the $92 mask, so only objects of those classes are disarmed.
The mask test is per record, so objects outside the three masked classes keep their collision byte.
Cleared and skipped records converge on the same advance.
The interpreter walks a descriptor stream terminated by $FFFE, where each record names its own destination object by address, so one table can initialize an arbitrary set of records.
Bit 0 of the second descriptor byte is consumed as a flag that presets field $23, and the remaining bits are shifted down into field $25.
Each record supplies two longs of bounds, a byte doubled into field $26, and a final byte that overwrites the $23 the flag may have set.
Referenced only by bosses/antroid_core.s, which is the ownership its name claims.
Referenced only by bosses/shellshogun_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/sniper_honeyviper_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/madam_barbar_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/joker_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/terobuster_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/flying_neo_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/xi_tiger_core.s, whose setup state consumes it.
Referenced only by bosses/deep_strider.s.
Referenced only by bosses/sharpssteel_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/entity_type_1c0_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/back_stringer_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/wolf_garopa_core.s.

The table's only consumer is debug/valkirie_composite_viewer.s, a handler that Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs. The actual Valkirie battle uses the two separate intro and effect tables below it, so the boss attribution was wrong.
Referenced only by bosses/z_leo_core.s.
Referenced only by bosses/valkirie_battle.s, which is what distinguishes it from the viewer table above.
The second table bosses/valkirie_battle.s consumes.
Referenced only by bosses/medusa.s.
Referenced only by bosses/sirene.s.
Referenced only by bosses/artemis_core.s; unlike its neighbours it is declared as bytes rather than words.
Referenced only by bosses/unidentified_seven_force.s.
Referenced only by bosses/valkirie_alternate.s, a third and separate Valkirie module.
Referenced only by bosses/sylpheed_core.s; it is the last descriptor table in the group.
A linear scan of sixteen contiguous enemy records with no wraparound, which the former comment claimed.
The loop stops at the first zero type word.
A found slot and an exhausted scan share this return, distinguished by the zero flag.
The same shape over four records from the shared entity slot; nothing in the code ties it to explosions specifically, so that claim was removed.
Four iterations rather than sixteen is the only difference from the enemy scan.
The same dual-purpose return convention.
The generic scan takes both the pointer and the count from its caller, which is why the player-effect entry directly above it consists only of loading those two registers.
Found and exhausted both return here; five callers rely on the zero flag to tell them apart.
The entry fixes A0 at the twenty-sixth entity record and performs 28 unrolled type-word probes through the fifty-third record.
Each occupied probe advances A0 by the $60-byte object stride; a zero type word returns with Z set and the free record in A0.
A negative type word ends the list, which is the $FFFF terminator every asset load list in the game closes with.

Eight absolute long pointers indexed by the record type shifted left two. Types 0 and 4 share the RAM code copier and types 1 and 5 the VRAM writer, so only six handlers fill the eight slots. This is the table the field_0 word of every asset load list selects.
The length comes from a word at the head of the payload, divided by four, so the copier moves whole longs and the payload must be long-aligned.
Types 1 and 5. Its destination is read with moveq #0 first, so the word stays a $0000xxxx VRAM address, in contrast to the RAM handlers which seed the register with -1.
The batch size is $200 bytes, and the loop repeats until the remaining count reaches zero.
Interrupts are masked at $2700 for the whole batch and the autoincrement is set to 2 each time, so the transfer cannot be interrupted between the control write and the data writes.
A plain long-write loop to the data port rather than DMA, which is why the interrupt mask is needed.
Type 2. The tile count is the first byte of the payload and the same word is rotated by eight to seed the codec bit state, so the count byte and the first bit-stream byte overlap.
Decode then pack, once per tile, with the destination advanced by the packer rather than here.
Type 3. Instruction for instruction the routine above it except that the per-tile tail is the VRAM writer rather than the RAM packer.
The VRAM counterpart of the decode-and-pack loop.

Type 6 of LoadObjDataHandlers. Its destination word is read after moveq #$FFFFFFFF, so it is sign-extended into $FFFFxxxx and the decoder writes to RAM; the type-7 handler beside it seeds with moveq #0 and builds a VDP write command instead. Across the whole source, 153 of the 157 type-6 records carry a mapping payload and 169 of the 193 type-7 records carry tile art, so the two handler names were the wrong way round. The parallel table Sys_DataLoaderHandlers names the same two slots Data_DecompressLZSSDirect and Gfx_DecompressLZSSToVRAMBatched, by destination, which settles it. This name has no address-derived legacy because the label was imported already named.
It repeats the LZSS block decoder until the source pointer reaches the end computed from the payload length word. Renamed with its parent.

Type 7 of LoadObjDataHandlers. It decodes each $400-byte block into GraphicsStagingBuffer and writes it to VRAM through the data port with interrupts masked, advancing the destination by $400 each time. Renamed with its counterpart for the reasons recorded there. This name has no address-derived legacy because the label was imported already named.
Each pass resets the staging pointer to GraphicsStagingBuffer, decodes one block, and writes it out, so the buffer is reused rather than filled once.
A full block is $100 long words, which is $400 bytes, and the VRAM destination advances by $400 after each one.
The remaining length is computed as the staging pointer minus $B400, the base of GraphicsStagingBuffer, halved, so the tail is written as words rather than longs.
The word-at-a-time tail loop, the only structural difference from the full-block path.
The asynchronous counterpart of LoadObjData: instead of calling a handler it parses one record into the DataLoader RAM block and returns, leaving Sys_DispatchDataLoader to run the handler later.
The tile count byte plus one and the rotated bit-stream word, the same header the synchronous type-2 and type-3 handlers read inline.
Bit 0 of the type word selects a zero-extended destination against the sign-extended one, which is exactly the VRAM against RAM distinction the handler table encodes.
With bit 1 clear the payload is uncompressed and its length is simply the leading word.
With bits 1 and 2 both set the header holds a length that is turned into an absolute end pointer and parked in DataLoaderCodecState, which is where the LZSS handlers read their stop address from.
A negative type word ends the list here too, and leaves DataLoaderControl holding the $FFFF the dispatcher tests for.
Called from Reset. It alternates handler and parser: run the handler for the record just parsed, parse the next, and stop when the parse returns $FFFF.
The type is doubled twice rather than shifted, but the effect is the same long index into the second handler table.
An empty DataLoaderControl returns without touching anything.

The second eight-entry table, slot for slot the same type meanings as LoadObjDataHandlers: RAM copy, VRAM transfer, tiles to RAM, tiles to VRAM, then the same pair repeated, then LZSS to RAM and LZSS to VRAM. Its names for slots 6 and 7 say destination, which is what showed the first table had the corresponding two names the wrong way round.
It copies two longs per iteration and subtracts 8, so the length must be a multiple of eight; a shorter length would overrun because the test is bhi rather than bcc.
Unrolled by two, which is why the decrement is 8 rather than 4.
The asynchronous counterpart of Gfx_LoadDataToVRAM: the same $200-byte batching, but each batch is queued as a DMA and waited on rather than written through the data port.
The same $200 batch size as the synchronous writer.
The queue routine advances the source and destination itself, so the loop only tracks the remaining count.
A spin on VDPTransferPending, which the VBlank handler clears, so this routine blocks until the next frame boundary for every batch.
Type 2 of the second table, and the same decode-and-pack pair as its synchronous twin.
The count is decremented once before the loop, so the stored length is a true tile count.
Type 3. It decodes into TileDMABatchBuffer sixteen tiles at a time and DMAs each batch, so the buffer never needs to hold the whole payload.
The batch is $10 tiles, and the byte length is the tile count shifted left five, which fixes a tile at $20 bytes.
The remaining count is reduced before the decode loop, so the final partial batch falls out naturally.
The same decode-and-pack pair, here filling the DMA buffer rather than the destination.
Every batch waits for the transfer to drain before the next decode, so decode and DMA never overlap.
The final batch is queued from the same buffer with the length left by the decode loop.
The routine does not return until the last DMA has completed.
The routine invokes LZSSDecomp with the destination already configured in a2.
It performs no VDP-port access or DMA setup, so the destination is not necessarily VRAM.
Type 6 of the second table, and the exact shape of LoadCompressedToRAM_BlockLoop: decode blocks until the source reaches the end pointer.
The routine decodes blocks into the FFB400 staging buffer and passes each block to Gfx_ExecuteDMATransfer.
It waits for transfer completion before decoding the next block, establishing the staged VRAM behavior omitted by the previous name.

Named by Sys_DispatchGameState. Its fifteen phase labels are not arbitrary: each is the target of a FrameTimingDebugFlag test that writes $C0420000 to the VDP control port and then a colour to the data port, which is a CRAM write to entry $21. With the flag set the backdrop changes colour at every phase boundary, so the border becomes a raster profile of the frame.
The first phase bar is a plain HUD strip write rather than a CRAM colour, so the sequence starts one instruction differently from the fourteen that follow.
Camera motion runs before collision, so the cached bounds the collision pass builds already reflect this frame camera delta.
Collision_UpdateSystem itself returns immediately while bit 7 of FrameControlFlags is set, which is how the hit-stop freeze suppresses it.
This phase covers four calls at once: the sprite priority buckets, the visible-object list cursor, the stage number conversion and the primary palette effect.
The player update and the weapon ammo regeneration share one phase, so the profile bar cannot separate them.
The object spawner runs after the player, so a spawn reacts to the position the player reached this frame.
Projectile_ProcessVisiblePool is the second of the two routines that read Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, the other being Sys_ProcessVisibleObjects.
The enemy spawn director and the transition buffers share this phase.
One call, the per-stage process dispatcher, which is the largest single phase in the loop.
Five calls share this phase: the secondary palette effect, the object count, the message sequencer, the HUD and the screen shake.
The only work is Sprite_RenderObjectList, so the name describes the phase rather than a routine of its own.
The fade update is also where the two PaletteFadeMaskStatus bits are consumed, each with a bclr that both tests and clears.

It writes $41 into GameplayControlFlags, which is bits 6 and 0 and notably not bit 7, so unlike the $80 that boss and stage code writes it does not stop the frame counter. It is the fallback taken when a completed fade has no exit mode to select.
GameplayExitMode selects the destination: 1 gives mode $2C with SFX 4, 3 gives $34, and anything else gives $68, while zero falls back to the write above.
The middle case of the three-way selection.
The default case, reached for every exit mode other than 0, 1 and 3.
Bit 7 of GameplayControlFlags skips this block entirely, which is what freezes the frame counter during a boss defeat or a stage end.

This branch is taken while FrameFreezeTimer is still counting, and the $80 it writes sets bit 7 of FrameControlFlags, which makes Collision_UpdateSystem return immediately and Player_Update render without updating. It marks the frame frozen, not active, so the former SetActiveFrame name inverted it. The four-frame hit-stop that Collision_CheckPlayerAgainstHostiles arms is what drives it.
Both the frozen and the running case converge on this single store.
GameplayControlFlags is ORed into FrameControlFlags every frame, so a $80 written anywhere in the game propagates into the freeze bit on the next pass.
A two-instruction mode setter with no sound, unlike its neighbour.
It tail-jumps into the sound queue with request 1, which is why it is separate from the plain setter above.
The routine indexes its table with StageTableIndex divided by two.
The table encodes decimal stages 1 through 50 in packed BCD and the results renderer consumes the stored byte as two digits.

Fifty bytes that convert a stage table index, halved, into a packed BCD stage number: 1 to 9 map to themselves and the tenth entry is $10, so the table is a decimal-to-BCD conversion rather than an ordering.
After checking the frame-processing flag, the routine initializes word_FFF758 to ED00.
Sys_UpdateObjectCount derives the visible-object count from that cursor; this routine performs no VDP access.
A frozen frame returns here without resetting the cursor, so the visible-object list of the previous frame is redrawn unchanged.
The count is the cursor advance divided by two, because the list holds one word per object, and its base $ED00 is the same constant the begin routine writes.
A frozen frame leaves the previous count in place, which pairs with the cursor not being reset.
It requires both bit 7 and bit 6 of GameplayControlFlags, so the $80 that stops the frame counter is not enough on its own; the pause display needs the $40 as well.
Four conditions share this return, including a held start button, which is what suppresses the graphic while the button is down.
Bit 4 of the VBlank counter gates the render, so the pause graphic blinks every sixteen frames. The second sprite record points at Z80_RAM as its art source.
The routine computes camera deltas, iterates the active visible-object list, and applies shared motion biases to object positions.
It also clamps player and object coordinates, so its behavior is object motion rather than a graphics-only scroll update.
It publishes the global sprite flip bits from the frame counter and computes both camera deltas against the previous frame in one place, so every object that follows the camera reads one shared pair.
Bits 6 and 7 of CameraMotionLockFlags zero the horizontal and the vertical delta independently, so a stage can lock one axis and let the other scroll.
With both deltas zero the routine takes a second, shorter loop that skips the camera-follow step entirely rather than adding zero to every object.

d5, d6 and d7 are loaded with 3, 2 and 0 and then used as register bit indices throughout, which is what makes bit 3 of the object flag byte the horizontal velocity, bit 2 the vertical and bit 0 the camera follow.
The player is handled before the loop and is not in the list, which is why it gets the bounded velocity helper and the playfield clamp that list objects do not.
An object whose whole flag byte is zero is skipped before any bit test.

This label is the target taken when the horizontal step is skipped, and the code at it applies the vertical velocity. The former ApplyHorizontalVelocity name described the step above it rather than the step it performs, which is one position out from the convention Physics_ApplyVelocityWithBounds_ProcessVertical follows in the same module.
The third step subtracts the horizontal camera delta and adds the vertical one, so an object that follows the camera moves with it horizontally and against it vertically.
Both an empty flag byte and a completed object converge on the loop tail.
The moving-camera path has its own return because the stationary path continues past it.
It loads only d5 and d6, not d7, because no camera-follow step runs on this path.
The player still gets the bounded velocity helper and the clamp, but not the position offset the moving path applies.
The same loop as the visible one with the third step removed.
The same one-position naming error as its counterpart in the moving loop: it is reached when the horizontal step is skipped and it applies the vertical velocity.
Three paths converge here, one more than in the moving loop because the vertical skip lands here directly.
The stationary path return, also reached when the visible count is zero.
The stage scroll delta is added to the object velocity, quartered first when bit 1 of PlayerActionStateFlags is set, so a state can weaken the conveyor effect without changing the stage.
The limit is negated rather than a second constant being read, so the clamp is symmetric by construction.
Both the clamped and the unclamped case converge on one add.
Correctly named for the step it performs, which is the convention the two Object_ApplyCameraMotion labels were corrected to match.
The vertical half is the horizontal half with a different limit variable and no scroll-bias quartering.
The vertical counterpart of the shared add.
Only the vertical skip reaches this return; the horizontal skip falls into the vertical half.

It applies the camera delta, not an arbitrary offset: the same subtract and add the visible loop performs inline, factored out for the player. Its guard is bit d7, which the caller loaded with 0, the camera-follow bit.
An object that does not follow the camera returns here untouched.
The shared camera-motion routine passes each active object in a5 to this helper.
It clamps horizontal and vertical coordinates according to global bound-enable bits without testing any projectile identity or type.
The routine writes four-word sprite descriptors sequentially into the FFA100 display-list buffer.
It terminates the list with FFFF and tail-calls Sprite_AppendOAMEntries; no entity velocity or friction value is read or updated.
Its secondary entry is called directly by DebugMenu_UpdateAndDispatch, confirming UI ownership.
The block contains one subsystem call, to UI_BuildHUDSpriteList.
It performs no motion, collision, acceleration, or entity-state operation before continuing to Player_Update.
The Xi Tiger transition route calls the HUD sprite-list builder and HUD renderer, then indexes the nine-entry Xi Tiger cutscene state table.
The earlier UpdatePhysicsAndHUD claim was already rejected because the routine invokes no physics, terrain, collision, or movement routine.
A two-instruction entry that loads the current object's position and falls into the shared tile probe.

The routine has no caller and no reference in the ROM. The absolute-address scan does report one match, at $02AECC, but that address is the first long of Projectile_CollisionSpriteFrames and the value $000144D6 there is sprite-frame data, not a pointer, so the match is a coincidence.
Twelve absolute references reach this two-instruction entry, which adds the caller's offset to the object position before the shared tile probe.
The shared probe converts a screen position into a layout index, reads the tile word, and returns the tile's height byte masked to even values in d2 with the raw word in d3.
Seven absolute references reach this helper, which snaps the object up to the eight-pixel grid and clears the vertical velocity.
The ceiling counterpart snaps downward instead, using the complement of the same three-bit remainder.

Unreferenced and absent from the ROM, unlike the two vertical alignment helpers directly above it, which the same scan finds at seven and several sites. It would have snapped the object horizontally to the eight-pixel grid on whichever side its travel direction implies.
The leftward half of that unreferenced pair.
The helper loads the layout and height-table pointers and the $80 screen bias, then falls straight into the probe below, so callers get both the setup and one probe from a single call.

This probe differs from Collision_CheckTerrainTile in two ways: it biases by the caller's d7 rather than a fixed $80, and it adds 8 to the height for tile bit 11 and $40 for bit 12, which is how sloped and doubled tiles are encoded.
Positions above screen Y $A0 return zero height without touching the layout at all.
The two tile flags are independent, so a tile can take both adjustments.
An empty tile and both flag outcomes share this return.
The projectile probe treats any height of $80 or more as no contact, inverting the test the wall checks use, so projectiles pass through the surfaces that stop entities.
The empty-tile and the too-high cases share this return with d2 zero.
The plain wall check probes eight pixels to each side at the object's own height and sets bit 2 or bit 3 of field 7 on contact.
The right probe runs whether or not the left one found a wall, so both sides can resolve in one call.
Both probes converge on this return.
The extended check adds a second probe on each side at a vertical offset that the entry above derives from the vertical velocity, and that the facing wrapper overrides with its own choice.
The offset probe runs only when the level probe found nothing, and it resolves the collision without setting the contact bit.
The right side repeats the same two-probe pattern.
The right offset probe likewise resolves without setting the contact bit.
A clear right side returns here; the resolving paths tail-call out instead.
The routine samples terrain at horizontal offsets -8, 0, and +8 along two lower Y offsets.
It dispatches terrain-angle response handlers and reads no player input or action-state index.
Enemy and projectile state machines call the same routine, so player ownership is not established.
The routine probes both horizontal sides at the entity center and at a velocity-selected vertical offset.
Generic enemies and projectiles call it, and it contains no boss type or boss-state check.

The second of five probes, at x+8 and y+$18. The two inner probes are called with bsr so the scan continues past them; the centre and the two outer probes are tail branches, so a hit there ends the scan.
At x+0 and y+$20, and reached both from a miss and from a hit on the right inner probe.
At x-8 and y+$20. Inner and outer name the vertical depth in this family, not a horizontal spread: both pairs sit at x±8 and the outer pair is eight pixels further from the entity centre.
The last probe, at x+8 and y+$20; a miss falls into the shared return.
Only the final probe reaches this return; every earlier hit leaves through a handler.

Instruction for instruction the same five probes as Physics_CheckLowerTerrain, with one difference: the centre and both outer probes first test the sign of $1C and return instead of resolving while the entity is rising. The two inner probes are resolved unconditionally in both routines, so the descending guard is not global.
Unguarded, exactly like its counterpart in Physics_CheckLowerTerrain.
The first of the three guarded probes: a negative $1C, which is a rising entity, returns without resolving the hit.
The same guard again, tested after the probe rather than before it, so the tile lookup still runs.
The third and last guarded probe.

The final right-outer tile miss and the three negative-velocity guards return here. Each guard tests $1C(a5) after a center or outer tile hit and skips lower-terrain handling while that word is negative.

The mirror of Physics_CheckLowerTerrain with the vertical offsets negated: the inner pair at y-$18 and the centre and outer probes at y-$20, in the same left-inner, right-inner, centre, left-outer, right-outer order.
At x+8 and y-$18, called with bsr like its lower counterpart.
At x+0 and y-$20.
At x-8 and y-$20.
At x+8 and y-$20; the fifth probe of the upper family.
Reached only when all five probes miss.

The upper family's guarded variant. It differs from Physics_CheckUpperTerrain only in testing the sign of $1C on the centre and outer probes, with the sense inverted against the descending variant: here a non-negative $1C returns. The inner probes are again unguarded.
Unguarded, matching the descending variant's treatment of the inner pair.
The bpl guard is the mirror of the descending variant's bmi.
The second guarded probe.
The third guarded probe.

The final right-outer tile miss and the three nonnegative-velocity guards return here. Each guard tests $1C(a5) after a center or outer tile hit and skips upper-terrain handling while that word is nonnegative.

Sets the floor contact, bit 0 of 6(a5), unconditionally, and adds bit 2 for tile angles below $80. Bit 2 is therefore the shallow half of the angle range rather than a separate surface, and Player_HandleFallingState_CheckUpperTerrain relies on its upper counterpart to tell an attachable ceiling from a plain solid one.
The angle is masked to $7E and anything from $40 up is answered by the plain surface snap, so only the lower half of the angle range reaches the table.

Twenty-four words, covering masked angles $00 to $2E. Its entries are measured from Physics_HandleLowerLeftInnerTerrain, the routine that immediately follows it, which is the pattern for every response table in the family: each is based on the next handler in the chain.

Unlike the centre and outer handlers it first rejects angles below $10 outright and sends angles from $C0 up to the left wall resolver, so the inner probes carry the wall cases that the outer probes never see.
Reached either from an angle below $10 after masking, which skips the contact flags entirely, or from the flag-setting tail.

Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleLowerRightInnerTerrain. Its slots 1 and 5 hold the left wall resolver, where the centre table holds the plain surface snap, which is the whole difference between an inner and a centre response.
The mirror of the left inner handler, differing only in resolving to the right wall.

The lower-right inner path indexes Physics_LowerRightInnerResponseTable with normalized D2, adds the Physics_HandleLowerLeftOuterTerrain base to the selected offset, then jumps through A4. Its preceding gates can set bits zero and two in 6(a5).
Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleLowerLeftOuterTerrain, with the right wall resolver where the left table has the left one.
The outer handlers have the short shape of the centre one: the contact bits and then the dispatch, with no wall cases.
The same mask and the same $40 cutoff as the centre dispatch.
Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleLowerRightOuterTerrain.
The last of the five lower handlers and identical in shape to the left outer one.
The mirror of the left outer dispatch.
Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleUpperCenterTerrain, so the chain of bases crosses from the lower family into the upper one here.

The angle test is the inverse of the lower centre handler's: below $80 it sets only the solid flag through Physics_SetSolidTerrainFlag and returns, and only from $80 up does it set bit 1 and dispatch. That split is what separates an attachable ceiling from a solid one everywhere in the player states.
Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleUpperLeftInnerTerrain. The upper index is the masked angle less $40, so the same twenty-four slots serve the upper half of the angle range.
The caller reaches this routine only after the upper-left inner terrain probe at offsets -8 and -24 succeeds.
The routine normalizes the terrain angle and dispatches a response table; it never writes either velocity field.
Entered both from an angle below $80 and from one at $C0 or above, so the wall resolver claims only the $80 to $BF band and everything else is normalised into the table index.
An index below $10 skips the ceiling contact bit, matching the lower inner handlers' treatment of shallow angles.
Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleUpperRightInnerTerrain, of which the last twelve are all the empty handler, so half the upper index range resolves to nothing.
The mirror of the upper left inner handler, resolving to the right wall.
The mirror of the left inner normalisation.

The upper-right inner path indexes Physics_UpperRightInnerResponseTable with normalized D2, adds the Physics_HandleUpperLeftOuterTerrain base to the selected offset, then jumps through A4. Its preceding gate can set bit one in 6(a5).
Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleUpperLeftOuterTerrain, again with twelve trailing empty entries.
The caller reaches this routine from the upper-left outer probe at offsets -8 and -32.
It sets collision flags and dispatches a terrain-angle response without adding to a velocity or acceleration value.

Twenty-four words based on Physics_HandleUpperRightOuterTerrain, which is the first routine of player/terrain_responses.s, so the base chain also crosses the module boundary. Its own table is the only one in the family based on Physics_TerrainEmptyHandler, because it ends the chain.

The tenth and last probe handler, and the only one outside player/terrain_collision.s. Its table is the only one in the family measured from Physics_TerrainEmptyHandler, because it ends the chain of bases rather than pointing at the next handler.
Twenty-four words, the same size as the other nine, and the last twelve are all the empty handler.
The base of the last response table and the target of most of its slots. Its address comes from build/main.lst, because nullsub names carry a counter rather than an address.
Two instructions that set bit 2 of 6(a5). That bit is what Player_HandleFallingState_CheckUpperTerrain reads to tell a solid ceiling from an attachable one.
The shared tail of every alignment core: it clears the vertical velocity and removes the sub-tile remainder of the Y position, so the entity lands on the tile boundary.
The upper mirror, negating and decrementing before the mask so the remainder is measured from the other side of the tile.

A wrapper: seed 8 through the half-step core at Physics_AlignToFloorWithOffset, which snaps to the lower surface and then subtracts (x and 7) shifted right one plus one from the seed, then $C subtracted from Y.
Seed 8 through the half-step core, then 4 subtracted.
Seed 8 through the half-step core, then 4 added.
Seed 8 through the half-step core, then $C added.
Seed 4 through the half-step core, then $C subtracted.
Seed 4 through the half-step core, then 4 subtracted.
Seed 4 through the half-step core, then $C added.
One of the two seeds for the half-step core at Physics_AlignToFloorWithOffset, which snaps to the lower surface and then subtracts (x and 7) shifted right one plus one from the seed.
The other seed for the same core, and the fall-through into it.
The half-step core. The plus one after the shift is what makes the alignment land a pixel inside the tile rather than exactly on its edge.
Seed 4 through the even core at Physics_AlignFloorEvenOffset, which adds (x and 6) shifted right one to the seed rather than subtracting, then 4 added.
Seed 4 through the even core, then $C subtracted.
Seed 4 through the even core, then 4 subtracted.
Seed 4 through the even core, then $C added.
Seed 0 through the even core, then 4 added.
Seed 0 through the even core, then $C subtracted.
Seed 0 through the even core, then 4 subtracted.
Seed 0 through the even core, then $C added.
One of the two seeds for the even core.
The other seed, and the fall-through into the core.
The even core. Its mask is 6 rather than 7 and it adds where the half-step core subtracts, so it is the only core that never produces a negative adjustment.

Seed 8 through the quarter-step subtracting core at Physics_AlignFloorQuarterSubtractOffset, which subtracts (x and 7) shifted right two plus one from the seed, then $A subtracted. Renamed from Prepare8Sub10, which named it as a seed when it is a wrapper.
Seed 8 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed 8 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 subtracted.

Seed 8 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 added. It was called Physics_SnapAndAdd2, which put it beside Physics_SnapAndAdd4; but that routine seeds the half-step core and this one the quarter-step core, so the two were never siblings.
Seed 6 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then $A subtracted.
Seed 6 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed 6 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 subtracted.
Seed 6 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 added.
Seed 4 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then $A subtracted.
Seed 4 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed 4 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 subtracted.
Seed 4 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 added.
Seed 2 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then $A subtracted.
Seed 2 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed 2 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 subtracted.
Seed 2 through the quarter-step subtracting core, then 2 added.
The first of four seeds for the quarter-step subtracting core.
This helper loads 6 into D3 and branches to Physics_AlignFloorQuarterSubtractOffset; Physics_ApplyOffset6Sub10 calls it before subtracting ten from Y.
The third seed. It was called Physics_ApplyFloorOffset4, which read as a wrapper, while its three siblings are all named Prepare; it does only the seed and the branch.
The quarter-step subtracting core. Its shift is two rather than one, so one adjustment step covers four pixels of horizontal travel against the half-step core's two.
Seed 5 through the quarter-step adding core at Physics_AlignFloorQuarterAddOffset, which adds the same term instead, then $A subtracted.
Seed 5 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 added.
Seed 5 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 subtracted.
Seed 3 through the quarter-step adding core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed 3 through the quarter-step adding core, then $A subtracted.
Seed 3 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 added.
Seed 3 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 subtracted.
Seed 1 through the quarter-step adding core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed 1 through the quarter-step adding core, then $A subtracted.
Seed 1 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 added.
Seed 1 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 subtracted.
Seed -1 through the quarter-step adding core, then 6 subtracted.
Seed -1 through the quarter-step adding core, then $A subtracted.
Seed -1 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 added.
Seed -1 through the quarter-step adding core, then 2 subtracted.
The first of four seeds for the quarter-step adding core.
This helper loads 3 into D3 and branches to Physics_AlignFloorQuarterAddOffset; Physics_ApplyOffset3Sub6 calls it before subtracting six from Y.
The third seed.
The fourth seed, negative one, and the fall-through into the core.
The quarter-step adding core, identical to the subtracting one except for the sign, which is why the seeds that feed it run 5, 3, 1 and -1 rather than 8, 6, 4 and 2.
The routine marks the right-side collision flag and subtracts the tile penetration depth from the entity X coordinate.
It accesses no sprite mapping, animation counter, or boss identity.
The routine invokes the shared floor-alignment calculation seeded with 4 and then adds 4 to the entity Y coordinate.
It is selected from generic terrain-angle response tables and contains no Destroyer MK2 state or type check.
This entry sets d3 to 2 and falls into the shared quarter-step floor-alignment calculation.
Four generic terrain response entries call it; no battle state or boss data is accessed.
All six wrappers in this group share one gate: bit 5 of PlayerRestrictionFlags suppresses terrain collision entirely. This one adds nothing else and tail-calls the plain wall check.
The same gate in front of the extended wall check; like the plain one it does not consult moving platforms.
The four vertical wrappers differ from the two wall wrappers by running Collision_CheckPlayerPlatforms first, so a moving platform is resolved before the terrain probe.
The descending variant selects the probe that only resolves contact while the player is moving downward.
The ceiling counterpart of the lower wrapper, used by every state in the ceiling block.
The rising variant resolves ceiling contact only while the player is moving upward.

The wrapper chooses the vertical probe offset from bit 4 of the byte at $E, the vertical flip, supplying $FFE8 when the player hangs the usual way up and $18 when he is inverted, then enters the extended wall check past its own offset setup.
All six wrappers return here when the restriction bit is set, which is the single point where terrain collision is disabled.

The routine converts the D-pad into an eight-way aim index in field $9E. It is inert while a script drives the player, and ShootingMode decides whether the fire button must be held or newly pressed for the aim to update.
In the other shooting mode the gate is the pressed byte rather than the held byte, so the aim latches on the press instead of tracking.
A left or right press sets the facing bit and clears the opposite direction bit, so the remaining nibble can never hold both horizontals at once.
The right test runs only when left was not pressed, so left wins a simultaneous press.
With no direction held the index comes from the facing alone, 0 for right and 4 for left, which are the same two values the table produces for those directions.
Any held direction is decoded through the sixteen-entry table indexed by the cleaned nibble.
Both paths converge to store the index in field $9E, which is the only consumer-visible output of the routine.
The scripted-player path returns here without touching the aim.

Sixteen bytes mapping the D-pad nibble to an eight-way index that runs clockwise from right: 0 right, 1 down-right, 2 down, 3 down-left, 4 left, 5 up-left, 6 up, 7 up-right. Entries for impossible combinations are zero.

The aim index drives the facing rather than the reverse. While the fire button is held in moving-shooting mode, a right-facing player flips once the index reaches the down-left to up-left range 3 to 5, and a left-facing player flips for right, down-right or up-right.
The left-facing half tests the two ends of the index range rather than a contiguous span, because right sits at index 0.
Both facings converge on a single toggle of the $800 horizontal-flip bit.
Fixed-shooting mode and a released fire button both leave the facing alone.
The routine exclusively reads and writes object offset 0x18, the horizontal 16.16 velocity paired with X at offset 0x10.
Facing bit 3 selects addition or subtraction of 0xA800 toward symmetric horizontal limits.
The leftward branch applies the shared $A800 step, and its limit is reached only when the velocity is already past $FFFBE000.
The rightward branch mirrors it against $42000, so this variant is symmetric at plus or minus $42000.
A velocity of the opposite sign always accelerates, so reversing direction is not limit-checked.
Both the accelerated and the clamped cases converge on one store.
The routine subtracts 0xA800 from object offset 0x18 toward a negative limit.
It does not access the vertical velocity at offset 0x1C, so neither downward motion nor gravity is implemented.
The armed leftward variant uses the same $A800 step but a lower limit of $FFFD6000.
This store writes unchanged D0 when the incoming horizontal velocity is strictly below -$2A000; otherwise the preceding path subtracts $A800. It does not clamp D0 to the threshold.
The routine adds 0xA800 to object offset 0x18 toward a positive limit.
It does not access the vertical velocity at offset 0x1C, so neither upward motion nor gravity is implemented.
After the common disable and moving-platform checks, facing bit 4 selects between lower- and upper-boundary terrain probes.
The routine neither reads directional input nor dispatches a player action state.
The routine enters the additive quarter-step alignment family through the helper that seeds d3 with 5.
After alignment it subtracts 6 from the Y coordinate; the previous name confused the adjustment with the seed and asserted a screen direction.

Player_Update calls this first; it leaves the cached input untouched while a script drives the player, and otherwise copies the held and pressed controller bytes into fields $69 and $6A through PlayerInputMask.
The scripted-player path returns here without touching the cached input bytes.

The routine clears bit 7 of the byte at $E, which is bit 15 of the sprite attribute word and therefore the priority bit, then merges GlobalSpritePriorityBit back in. It sets no direction: the horizontal facing bit is $800, and Player_UpdateHorizontalFacing owns it.
The routine returns unchanged while bit 5 of PlayerActionStateFlags is set.

A nonzero selector in $5C picks one of seven long entries from Player_HitboxBoundsTable, is consumed, and the result is stored in $28. When bit 4 of the byte at $E is set, which is the vertical flip, the first two bytes are swapped and negated through the two mirror scratch words first.
The routine stores the selected or horizontally mirrored four-byte hitbox boundary value at object offset 0x28.
It performs no arithmetic or coordinate write, so the previous claim that it applies an offset was inaccurate.

Two stage-entry paths call this. It installs the player object's type, flags, hitbox and draw bucket, seeds PhoenixAttackStatus at $78, sets both physics velocity limits to $74000, and tail-calls the weapon state machine.
The frozen-frame path returns here, and Player_StateHandlerOffsets also names this label for three separate state slots, so it doubles as the idle state handler.

The gameplay loop calls this. Bit 1 of PlayerModeFlags erases the object entirely, a negative frame-control flag renders without updating, and two further mode bits divert to the Seven Forces battle updates before the ordinary path runs.
An exhausted stage timer and zero health both enter the defeat exit through the same call, so the two lose conditions share one path.
Bit 1 of the contact byte moves the player into the forced-position state, which is how a cutscene takes control.
The pit death at Y $171 is suppressed while the player is already in the death state $36, while rising, and while bit 0 of PlayerRestrictionFlags is set.
The Counter Force input is sampled immediately before the state machine runs, so a state can act on it in the same frame.

Whether or not a state ran, the update ends by refreshing the sprite priority bit, caching the previous input byte in $6B, spending the invulnerability timer, selecting the hitbox and recomputing the centre position.
The dispatcher indexes 48 words measured from Player_HandleDeathSequence, which is why an absolute-address scan finds no player state handler at all.

The 48 offsets resolve into three groups: grounded states $00 to $16, the airborne and knockback states, and the ceiling block $18 to $26 audited separately. Several slots repeat one handler and three name the shared return.

The base label the whole state table is measured from. It plays SFX $2B, restricts the input mask to $73, pins the player at Y $120, saves the attribute byte and draw bucket for the respawn to restore, and arms a $A0-frame countdown.
State $36 drains health by one or two units per frame depending on a frame-counter bit, so the bar empties at an uneven rate.
The second decrement is unconditional and the result is clamped at zero.
Pressing any of the three $70 buttons plays SFX $BD and spends one of three retries, so the countdown can be cut short three times before the respawn begins anyway.
Every frame that does not end the countdown renders the death particles.
The respawn restores the saved attribute byte and draw bucket, places the player at Y $170 with an upward velocity, and selects state $38.
State $38 accumulates gravity and clears both air-move flags once the velocity turns positive, then joins the ordinary falling state's terrain handling.

The routine writes state $00. That state calls Physics_LowerTerrainCheckWrapper and diverts to Player_InitFallState the moment ground contact is lost, so it is the grounded standing state and the former air name was wrong.
The weapon-select and special-move guards of the standing state share this bare return.

State $00 is where the player stands: it requires ground contact, spawns the idle particle, and routes a held down to the crouch and a held direction to the ground direction selector, otherwise rendering the idle frame.
The directional tests are skipped entirely while the fire button is held in fixed-shooting mode, which is what lets the player shoot without turning.
Bit 4 of the cached input selects the special-weapon pose over the idle frame.
The entry arms a two-frame counter and falls into the shared tail, which writes state $0E.
Four other states enter here directly with their own counter, which is why the entry above is only two instructions.
The crouch state's two input guards share this bare return.

State $0E also requires ground contact and falls to Player_InitFallState without it. It decelerates, and once its counter expires a released down button returns the player to standing, so it is the crouch rather than an airborne state.
Holding the fire button in fixed-shooting mode keeps the crouch alive regardless of the down button.
Both the timer path and the still-held path converge on the armed or unarmed rendering choice.
The routine writes state $0A, which is the grounded deceleration rather than a jump.

State $0A requires ground contact, brakes the horizontal velocity, and once stopped either routes a held direction to the ground direction selector or returns the player to standing. It mirrors the ceiling deceleration state exactly.
The two input guards of the deceleration state share this return, and the landing state reuses it.
The landing entry plays SFX $B1 and arms two separate counters, one for the pose and one for the input window.
State $16 is the landing recovery: it decelerates with a gentler $4000 step than the deceleration state and spends both counters at once.
A held direction leaves through the ground direction selector, and no direction at all enters the deceleration state.
The mid-counter frames and the crouch-started path share the armed or unarmed rendering choice.

The selector is reached from the standing state with a direction held. It compares the held direction with the facing bit and enters the armed ground-weapon state when they agree, or the grounded movement state, which turns the player, when they do not.
The deceleration and landing states enter here instead; the only difference is that fixed-shooting mode returns the player to standing rather than simply returning.
The right-hand half of the agree-or-turn comparison.
The left-hand half, whose no-direction case falls back to the deceleration state.
The routine writes state $02, which Player_StateHandlerOffsets resolves to Player_GroundedMovementState, and ends in the automatic facing flip. It performs no wall bounce.
The two input guards of the grounded movement state share this bare return.
The routine is a player state-table target that checks lower terrain contact, movement input, jumps, and player special moves.
It neither accesses a boss object nor reads or writes a health value.

The routine has no caller, its absolute address does not occur in the ROM, and resolving the 48 words of Player_StateHandlerOffsets against Player_HandleDeathSequence does not produce its offset either, while the live states in the same module do resolve. Its body repeats the health-minus-maximum store that Player_UpdateCounterForceInput ends with and returns 1 in d0.
Both input guards of that unreachable routine return here with d0 untouched.
The entry arms a two-frame counter and falls into the animation half, so callers that already set their own counter enter one instruction later.
The shared half selects state $22, sets the vertical flip, masks the Start button out of the input, and ends in the automatic facing flip.
A bare return taken when the ceiling weapon selector consumed the input.
The dash decelerates every frame and, once its counter underflows, either continues while the fire button is held in fixed-shooting mode or drops back to the ceiling idle state.
Releasing the up direction ends the dash; holding it keeps the state alive with a pinned counter.
Bit 4 of the cached input selects the armed or unarmed rendering path, the same test every ceiling state uses.

The routine selects state $1E, which Player_StateHandlerOffsets resolves to the handler below. That handler tests upper-terrain contact and routes to the ceiling idle and ceiling counter-force states, so it is a ceiling state and not a ground crouch.

State $1E brakes the horizontal velocity while the player hangs from the ceiling. While it is still sliding it renders the movement pose; once stopped it enters ceiling movement if a direction is held and the ceiling idle state otherwise.
The still-sliding path renders either the armed grounded frame or the common movement mapping pair.
The weapon-selector and dash-input paths of the braking state share this return, which its neighbours reuse.
After the landing timer expires a held direction enters ceiling movement and no direction enters the braking state.
The landing frames and the dash-started path share the armed or unarmed rendering choice.

Every path through this routine ends at an entry that writes state $1A, which Player_StateHandlerOffsets resolves to Player_CeilingMovementState. It performs no wall kick; the former name named a move that does not exist here.
The braking state and the ceiling landing state enter here when a direction is held; it differs from the entry above only in returning to the ceiling idle state when fixed-shooting mode is active.
A held right direction enters the air-control state when the player already faces right, and otherwise turns him first.
The mirrored left test, whose no-direction case falls back to the braking state.
The shared tail masks the Start button out of the input, writes state $1A with a four-frame counter, and ends in the automatic facing flip.
A bare return shared by the weapon-selector and dash-input paths of the ceiling movement state.
The routine is a player state-table target that checks upper terrain contact and handles directional movement, dash, counter, and crouch transitions.
It does not call the sound driver or inspect any boss damage state.
The armed rightward variant mirrors it against $2A000, so the armed pair tops out at plus or minus $2A000, well below the by-facing pair.
This store writes unchanged D0 when the incoming horizontal velocity is at least +$2A000; otherwise the preceding path adds $A800. It does not clamp D0 to the threshold.
A one-instruction entry that presets the $C000 deceleration step and falls into the general routine, which callers can also enter directly with their own step in d1.
The routine moves the velocity toward zero by the caller's step and snaps to exactly zero whenever the step would cross it, so it never oscillates around the origin.
The negative half adds the step instead of subtracting it and applies the same crossing test.
Both signs converge on one store; the two snap-to-zero paths store separately because they clear d0 first.
Four signed byte pairs cycled on bits 2 and 3 of the frame counter, which is what gives the idle pose its slow breathing motion.
A negative animation counter selects the cycling offsets; the jump apex state enters here directly to force them.
A non-negative counter uses a fixed offset pair and the common movement mapping instead.
Four signed byte pairs cycled on bits 2 and 3 of the frame counter, the counterpart of the idle table but with much larger vertical offsets. Renamed with the routine that is its only reader.
Both ordinary grounded and ceiling player movement states tail-call the routine after processing directional input.
It advances a repeating eight-frame cycle and submits player sprite pieces; no boss or death condition is tested.
This helper seeds X offset D0 to -4 and X velocity D2 to -$40000, chooses Y offset -10 or +10 from player flag bit four, then branches to Player_CreateCounterForceEffect.
The facing bit is rewritten from the held direction before the frame timer is touched, so a turn shows on the same frame it is input.
Every fourth frame the animation index advances by four and wraps inside the $1C mask, giving an eight-frame walk cycle.
SFX $D6 plays on exactly two of the eight frames, indices 0 and $10, which are the two footfalls of the cycle.
Both streams are indexed with the same value, so the primary and secondary tables are parallel.
Eight long pointers, one per walk frame.
The parallel eight-entry secondary table, which the dash animation also reads with its own index.

Its only caller is Player_CeilingAirControlState, and it loads muzzle offset set 2. Across this module the offset set encodes orientation: sets 2 and 3 are used exclusively by ceiling states and sets 0 and 1 exclusively by ground states, which is what separates this routine from the one directly below it.
The ground counterpart, called by Player_GroundWeaponState and loading offset set 0. The former Render and Prepare names described no difference between the two.
Both weapon poses share this six-frame cycle, which advances every fifth frame, wraps at $18, and plays SFX $D6 on indices 0 and $C.
The sound test uses the index from before the advance, so it fires on the frame being left rather than the one being entered.
The same SFX $D6 the walk cycle uses, on two of the six frames.
The mapping pointer and the tile offset come from two parallel tables indexed by the same value halved for the word table.
Six signed word offsets that shift the weapon tiles by one pixel on four of the six frames.
Six long pointers; the sixth reuses the dash secondary mapping rather than having its own.
Called only by Player_CeilingIdleState when the fire button is held, and loading offset sets 2. It renders an idle pose rather than a dash, which the former name claimed.
Fixed-shooting mode takes the primary layout instead of the alternate one, the same choice every armed renderer in this module makes.
The ground counterpart, called by Player_GroundIdleState under the same condition and loading offset sets 0.
The ground fixed-shooting variant.
Called by the ceiling dash and ceiling landing states, loading offset sets 3, and falling back to the ceiling motion frame when the animation counter is non-negative.
The fixed-shooting variant of the ceiling armed motion pose.
Its callers are Player_GroundCrouchState and Player_HandleLandingState, both of which require ground contact, and it loads offset sets 1. The former airborne name was wrong on both counts.
The fixed-shooting variant of the ground armed motion pose.
The unarmed fallback of the ceiling armed motion pose, also called directly by Player_CeilingDecelerateState, and loading offset set 2. Its former grounded name contradicted both callers.
The ground counterpart, called by Player_GroundDecelerateState and by the ground armed motion pose, loading offset set 0. It renders no fall; the falling state has its own renderer.
Both call sites are in Player_CeilingMovementState and it loads offset set 2.
Both call sites are in Player_GroundedMovementState and it loads offset set 0, completing the ceiling and ground pairing across all seven renderer families.
Both dash poses share this cycle, which advances every fourth frame inside the $1C mask and plays SFX $D6 on indices 0 and $10, exactly like the walk cycle.
The two footfall frames of the dash cycle.
The dash reuses the walk cycle's secondary frame table rather than having its own, and only the tile offsets differ.
Eight signed word offsets, against the weapon cycle's six, because the dash follows the eight-frame walk table.
The helper advances the frame and then applies the automatic facing flip only when field $52 is clear, so a state can suppress the turn by setting it.
The frame index is taken from the caller's d1 offset into the shared animation frame table.
Eight long pointers that the plus-four and minus-four state thunks index from opposite directions.
The death state calls this every frame it is not ending; it walks a fixed particle set rather than allocating objects.

Player_RenderDeathParticles calls Player_WriteDeathParticleSprite for each d0 iteration and repeats until d0 becomes negative; Player_DeathSequenceAnimationFrames is indexed only after particle OAM is appended.
Player_RenderDeathParticles first appends particle OAM, then masks FrameCounter to $1C and indexes these eight longwords to write a death-sequence mapping pointer into player field 8(a5).
The writer bypasses the ordinary sprite-piece builder, which is why the death particles are unaffected by the layout tables.
The common entry selects the primary layout table before falling into the shared body.
Callers that already chose a layout table, which in this module means every fixed-shooting variant, enter here instead.
The frame index comes from the terrain animation tables, which is where the lower and upper terrain index tables in player/projectiles_and_effects.s are consumed.
The layout table used by the default rendering path.
The layout table used whenever moving-shooting mode is active, selected by every armed renderer in this module.

This constructor sets palette-adjust fields, writes $1CC, the Counter Force animation pointer, and value eight at object field $48 into PlayerSpecialObjectSlot, and flips X offset and velocity according to facing before placement.
The teleport-dash projectile costs health: the default difficulty spends $1E and the other $32, and each path posts the amount to HealthDeltaDisplayValue with a $30-frame timer.
The non-default difficulty branch differs only in the health cost and the projectile's own lifetime field.

The routine has no caller and its absolute address does not occur in the ROM, while Effect_SpawnParticle in the same module is found by that scan. It begins with a conditional branch, so it also depends on condition codes a caller would have set.
The second half of that unreachable pair derives a four-entry frame offset from the frame counter.
The routine expands two terminated frame streams into the buffer at 0xFF8780 while applying tile and coordinate offsets.
It is called by many ordinary player animation paths and does not update stage progression or a boss state.
The primary stream is copied piece by piece until a terminator bit is found in the first word of a piece, with the caller's d5 and d6 biasing the tile and attribute fields.
The terminating piece is still copied, and its packed size byte is decoded into a tile count that advances the base index for the secondary stream.
The secondary stream is appended with every tile index shifted by that accumulated count, which is how two independent mappings share one tile allocation.

The jump and ceiling states call this. It suppresses the particle while the input bit 4 is held and on seven of every eight frames, then gives the particle a random direction whose two axes are scaled by two independently drawn shift amounts.
Both branches of the vertical-flip test load the same $10 bias, so the particle box is the same whichever way the player faces.
The held-input, off-frame and no-free-slot cases share this return.

One external caller reaches this routine. It emits one particle every other frame, drains PhoenixAttackStatus by two per emission without letting it go negative, and plays SFX $AC every sixteenth frame.
The sound is tied to the frame counter rather than the particle count, so it stays at a fixed rate.
Each particle is placed eight times further along its own velocity vector than the velocity itself, so the effect trails behind the player rather than starting at him.
The off-frame, held-input and no-free-slot cases share this return.
The special attack fires three shots $40 angle units apart, starting from $C0 or $1E0 depending on facing, with the muzzle offset eight pixels to the matching side.
The leftward variant mirrors both the start angle and the muzzle offset.
Three iterations share one initializer, which advances the destination pointer itself, so the caller never has to.

Unreferenced and absent from the ROM as an absolute address. Unlike the triple shot directly above it, this five-shot variant never loads a0 with the effect pool, so it would also depend on a caller's register state.
Five iterations $40 angle units apart, with a speed shift of four against the triple shot's three.
The shared initializer converts the angle in d6 into a velocity scaled by d5, places the shot eight pixels above the player at the horizontal position in d4, and advances a0 to the next record.
Eight animation indices selected while the player stands on lower terrain.
The ceiling-attached counterpart, whose two halves are the lower table's halves exchanged.

The routine has no caller and its absolute address does not occur in the ROM, while Effect_SpawnParticle in the same module is found by that scan. It is also the only reader of HealthDeltaDisplayValue and HealthDeltaDisplayTimer, which three live sites still write: the health pickup, the contact-damage path, and the teleport-dash health cost.
The routine clears only the first two words of the player object: its identifier and display-attribute word.
No state-machine field or broader player state block is cleared.
The only object mutation is setting bit 7 of display word 2, the same bit cleared by the invulnerability blink renderer.
The routine does not update the invulnerability timer or collision flags.

The grounded state checks wall and floor contact, changes to airborne Counter Force when floor contact is lost, expires timer $4A to ground idle, or decelerates and renders after the dash-input check.
The airborne state adds $5000 to vertical velocity, checks walls and descending or rising terrain according to velocity sign, lands on floor contact, then reaches the Counter Force timer path.
Newly pressed input bit five and held bit one must both be set; then this helper stores PlayerHealth minus PlayerMaxHealth in PhoenixAttackStatus and sets D0 to one.

The state this render path belongs to requires ground contact and exits to Player_InitFallState the moment it is lost, so the block renders a grounded slide rather than air movement. It is reached only while the horizontal velocity is still non-zero.
The selector-start path converges at this return with D0 set to one; its second held-down test follows an earlier down+A diversion on the ordinary entry path.
The routine selects cyclic coordinate offsets and fixed player frame streams before tail-calling Player_BuildSpritePieces.
It performs no collision query, health update, or knockback mutation.

Six call sites reach this renderer and only one of them, the jump apex, is airborne. The other five are the ceiling dash, the ceiling landing, the grounded crouch, the grounded landing and the slide, all of which require ceiling or ground contact. It is the shared pose for states in motion, as opposed to Player_RenderIdleFrame, so the airborne attribution was wrong. This record supersedes the earlier confirmation, which was made before the grounded state family was corrected.

Two paths reach it: Player_DropFromCeiling, and Player_CeilingIdleState the moment the ceiling-attach contact bit 1 of 6(a5) is lost. Neither is a dash ending. It clears PlayerAirMoveUsedFlags and the animation accumulator $52 before falling into the state-$28 entry below.

The field-for-field twin of Player_InitFallState_Finish: the same CounterForceTriggerFlag clear, the same bclr #4,$E ceiling-attachment clear, the same $C animation request, the same $48 and $4A seeds and the same $7F input mask. It differs only in writing state $28 instead of $06 and in adding a downward $12000 push. Player_DashAttackState_ExitToFall chooses between the two on exactly that attachment bit, which is what identifies $28 as the ceiling-detach fall.

Player_StateHandlerOffsets names this handler in four separate slots, $06, $08, $14 and $28, so the slot value carries the entry's intent while the behaviour is shared. It is also entered directly from Player_KnockbackState.

While $48 is non-negative both of its branches skip the gravity add, so gravity is suppressed for the whole window. The two instructions above set $48 to -1 the moment bit 5 of $69, the C button, is released, which makes $48 the remaining jump-hold frames and this the variable jump height.
Gravity is $8800 per frame, the same step Player_UpwardTerrainLaunchState uses.
The wall check runs unconditionally and the sign of $1C then selects the rising or the descending vertical probe. Player_HandleRespawnGravity jumps in here to reuse both.
While $4A is non-negative the lower probe is skipped entirely, so the field is a countdown of frames during which the player cannot land.
Bit 0 of 6(a5) is the floor contact the lower probe sets, and it leads straight to the landing state.

The two upper bits are distinct surfaces: bit 1 is set only for tile angles at or above $80, the attachable ceiling, and sends the player to Player_InitCeilingLandingState; bit 2 comes from Physics_SetSolidTerrainFlag for shallower angles and, with up held, sends the player to Player_InitUpwardTerrainLaunch.
The Counter Force trigger is tested before the C button, so it wins over both the special attack and the dash.
Down plus C reaches the dash, which is refused once PlayerAirDashUsedFlag is set, so each airborne stretch allows one dash.
A non-zero $52 forces the ordinary air control; only with $52 clear does bit 4 of $69, the shot button, divert to the locked-facing control.
The ordinary path lets Player_ApplyAirControl rewrite the facing bit, then renders through the fall frame selectors unless $52 is still counting.

This branch runs while the shot button is held and, unlike Player_ApplyAirControl, never touches bit 3 of $E, so the player keeps facing where it was firing. The former manual-control name described no difference from the routine it replaces.

The cap is $38000 when bit 3 of $E is clear, that is when the player already faces left, and only $2C000 when it faces right. With the right-hand half doing the mirror image, the locked-facing control caps backward movement lower than forward movement.
A velocity already past the cap is replaced by it rather than stepped further.
The step is $7777 per frame, the same magnitude Player_ApplyAirControl uses.
Left is tested first, so holding both directions moves the player left.
The mirrored cap: $38000 when bit 3 of $E is set and $2C000 when it is clear.
The mirror of the left-hand clamp.
The mirror of the left-hand step.

With no direction held the sign of the current velocity re-enters the opposite accelerate path, so the same $7777 step bleeds the velocity back toward zero. It tests the velocity rather than checking for a neutral one, which is what the former name claimed.
The locked-facing path renders through Player_PrepareSpriteRendering with muzzle offset set 0 of the primary layout, matching the ground renderers in player/rendering_and_defeat.s.
Both a rising velocity and a downward velocity below 3 take the ordinary mapping, so only a genuinely fast fall gets its own primary frame.
Called twice per frame of the falling state, once on the air-control path and once on the locked-facing path, and it selects only the secondary mapping in a2.
The negation makes the two thresholds below a test of the speed band rather than of the direction.

Both outer bands arrive here: a speed of 7 or more and a speed below 2. Only the middle band, 2 to 6, reaches the falling and rising poses, so this mapping is the default and the former fast-frame name covered half of its callers.
Inside the middle band the sign of $1C separates the rising pose from the falling one.

Its one caller reaches it only while the player is rising into upper terrain that Physics_SetSolidTerrainFlag marked as too shallow to attach to, with up held. It snaps the player up to the tile boundary through Physics_AlignToTerrain, then sets $1C to $FFF86000, which is eight pixels per frame upward, not downward as the former hard-landing name and comment claimed, and enters state $12.

State $12, whose only writer is the launch entry above. It carries the upward velocity against $8800 of gravity while running both vertical probes, so it can end in a floor landing, a ceiling attach, or, once the animation accumulator passes $38, an ordinary fall. Nothing in it bounces.
Only the attachable ceiling bit is tested here; the solid bit that started the launch is ignored, so the player is not relaunched by the same surface.
The accumulator starts at 6 and Player_AdvanceAnimationFrame adds 2 each frame, so the state gives up after 25 frames and the eight-entry frame table wraps three times inside that window.
Unlike the locked-facing control above it, this path rewrites bit 3 of $E from the held direction and uses one symmetric $38000 cap for both sides.
Reached both from the left input and, through the neutral handler, from a rightward velocity with no input.
Left is tested first here too.
The mirror of the left-hand accelerate.
The same bleed-to-zero shape as the locked-facing control's neutral handler.
Every branch of the routine converges on this single store.

Reached only from the falling state, on a C press without down and with PlayerAirShotUsedFlag clear, which it then sets. It quarters the horizontal velocity, launches upward at $18000, clears eight object blocks of PlayerEffectObjectPool, plays SFX $B0 and tail-calls Player_SpawnTripleShot.
State $4E, the value the init above writes, named by Player_StateHandlerOffsets. Its own $4C counter runs for five frames before the state hands over to Player_SpecialMoveRecoveryState.
Bit 6 of PlayerActionStateFlags is set only here, and gravity is $C000 rather than the falling state's $8800.
Only the attachable ceiling bit is tested; the solid bit has no upward launch path during the special attack.
A C press cancels the attack into a fall unless down is held and the air dash is still available.
The cancel leaves with an upward $80000 and $52 set to $FFE0, then joins Player_InitFallState_Finish, so it becomes state $06 rather than the ceiling-detach state $28.
Bit 0 of the frame counter alternates the two secondary mappings every frame, so the attack flickers between them rather than running a timed cycle.
Bit 4 of $69, the shot button, selects the armed branch, matching the render choice every other player state makes.
The player state table selects this routine for state 0x46 after Player_HandleSpecialAttack transfers into it.
It performs player terrain, input, damage, velocity, and rendering decisions and never iterates or updates particle objects.
Both the already-used air dash and the downward-held case converge here to take the faster $FFF80000 rise instead of the slower value the unreachable entry above would set.

The player state table holds word offsets from Player_HandleDeathSequence, and no entry resolves to this address; nothing branches to it either, while the control states Player_KnockbackState and Player_SpecialMoveRecoveryState are both found in that table. The single instruction sets the slower $FFFD8000 rise velocity before the live tail below.
This tail is live: the fast-velocity path branches straight to it. It stores the $FFE0 recovery marker in $52 and enters the shared fall state, so it no longer carries the unreachable entry's name.
The routine selects player frame streams and either builds the composite sprite or prepares the weapon overlay.
No availability, resource, or attack-state condition is checked.
Both frame-counter halves converge here with a secondary mapping chosen, and the held bit 4 then decides between the plain pose and the weapon overlay.
