The weapon path supplies the alternate muzzle offsets and layout table to the shared table-driven renderer instead of building the plain pose.
A bare return taken when the recovery weapon-select helper reports that it consumed the input.
During special-move recovery, pressed bit six gates selection; held down bit one calls the shooting-mode toggle, otherwise negative WeaponStateCooldown permits the recovery selector start.
State $54 sets action flags, checks floor and ceiling terrain, changes to recovery state $46 when WeaponStateIndex falls below $12, then renders the selection pose.
The invulnerable path reaches here every frame but plays SFX $19 only on every eighth, then installs the $FFFEA000 rise and prefers a stored horizontal knockback when one exists.
Both vertical variants share this path, which copies PlayerKnockbackXVel straight into the horizontal velocity.
With no stored knockback the default path installs $FFFF7000 and negates it unless the facing bit $800 is set, so the player is always pushed backwards.
The facing branch returns here once the sign is chosen.
The non-invulnerable path always plays SFX $19 and uses the stronger $FFFE8000 rise; it also tests only the low word of PlayerKnockbackXVel before falling through to the facing helper.

Unreferenced and absent from the player state table. The routine begins with a conditional branch, so it depends on condition codes the caller would have set, and selects $38000 or $FFFC8000 accordingly.
The negative half of that unreferenced pair.
The live facing-based variant, reached from the alternate vertical path: it installs $FFFC8000 and negates it unless the facing bit is set.
The sign-selection return of that live helper.
Player_InitKnockbackState assigns state 0x2A, whose state-table entry is this routine.
It applies knockback gravity and terrain collision before restoring normal player state; no death transition is performed.
While the knockback timer runs the state adds $6000 of gravity, checks walls, and only tests the lower terrain once the vertical velocity has turned positive.
While still rising the state tail-calls the rising-terrain wrapper instead, so ceilings are tested on the way up and floors on the way down.
A single nop with no reference anywhere and no entry in the player state table. Only the return instruction after it is live.
The knockback state branches here when the descending terrain check reports no contact, so this return is live even though the nop above it is not; the name now says which state uses it.
Both knockback exits call this helper, which clears PlayerDefeatPhase and restores the object flags and collision byte the hit had changed.
A bare return with no reference and no player state table entry; the prefix now records that directly rather than only in the name.
The initializer assigns state 0x18, whose handler probes upper terrain and exits when upper contact is lost.
The state is therefore the upper-terrain idle path, not a lower-terrain grounded state.
This bare return is live: the ceiling idle state branches to it from two separate input tests.
The routine is state 0x18 and begins by checking upper terrain contact before processing ordinary counter, dash, and movement input.
It is entered by Player_InitCeilingIdleState and is not itself the dash-state initializer.
The ceiling idle state reaches this block once the earlier input tests fall through, and it decides whether the dash state is entered.
The state converges here to build its sprite pieces when no input changed the state.
The ceiling state checks wall and upper-terrain contact, changes to airborne Counter Force if terrain bit one clears, expires timer $4A to ceiling idle, or decelerates and renders.
Player_InitDashState assigns state 0x22, whose state-table entry is this routine.
The routine requires upper-terrain contact, processes dash input and decelerates horizontal velocity before rendering.
Upper-terrain collision branches from falling and bounce states enter this initializer, which sets orientation bit 4 and state 0x26.
The corresponding handler begins with an upper-terrain probe.
The player state table maps state 0x26, assigned by Player_InitCeilingLandingState, to this routine.
It validates upper-terrain contact and runs a landing timer; it is not the general jump handler.
This state returns to ceiling idle when WeaponStateIndex falls below $12; otherwise it checks wall and upper contact, detaches into fall on lost terrain bit one, or renders idle.
The ceiling-mode entry XORs ShootingMode with 2, queues SFX $A3, and returns zero without writing PlayerInputMask.
Player_CheckCeilingWeaponSelectInput branches here when A and the up-direction bit are held.
With no direction held the state falls through to its own deceleration rather than changing state.
A held direction that matches the current facing accelerates; one that opposes it turns the player instead.
The mirrored right-hand test of that same choice.
The armed variant writes state $1C and clears its counter, and falls straight into the shared return below.
The initializer and the two input guards of the air-control state share this return.
State $1C is the armed counterpart of ceiling movement: it renders the weapon sprite every frame and drops back to the unarmed animation as soon as the fire button is released.
The right-hand half of its turn-or-accelerate choice, whose no-direction case enters the braking state.
State $48 reads the raw controller rather than the cached input bytes and sets only the flip bits, so it aims without moving.
The right test runs only when left is not held, so left wins a simultaneous press.
Neither direction held leaves the facing unchanged.
The routine is a one-instruction state-table thunk to Player_InitCeilingIdleState.
It does not inspect, update, or render weapon data.
State $4C applies a large $8800 gravity step and hands over to the fall state as soon as the velocity turns positive, so it occupies only the top of the arc.
State $50 teleports the player to a fixed point at X $78, restricts his input to the direction bits, clears the object blocks, and creates the type-$230 companion object that the dash trail follows.
State $52 decays both velocity components every frame and creates one dash trail per frame while the counter stays clear.
The finish clears the restriction flag and the two temporary collision bits, then installs the exit velocity and enters the shared fall tail.
This player state-table handler loads d1 with 4 and tail-calls Player_UpdateAnimationState.
It allocates no projectile and contains no Artemis-specific access.
State $5A is the negative counterpart of the state two entries below it; both are two-instruction thunks into the shared animation-state helper.
The routine is a player state-table entry that advances the player state, resets object blocks, and installs teleport-dash coordinates and frames.
It neither waits for VBlank nor references credits data.

Its only caller is Player_CheckDashInput, which is itself called only by Player_CeilingIdleState and Player_CeilingDecelerateState, and it is reached on a C press without up held; up plus C goes to the dash instead. It detaches from the ceiling and overrides the fall entry's push with a downward $20000, so it drops the player off the ceiling rather than ending a dash. This record supersedes the earlier confirmation, which was made before the ceiling-detach fall state was identified.
The routine initializes player state 0x14, which maps to the common Player_HandleFallingState handler, with a timer and vertical velocity.
It references no stage identifier, Gusthead object, or intro state.
The routine compares the player's vertical velocity and returns one of two player frame pointers in a1.
It writes no sprite or UI buffer and reads no boss health value.
The active special-attack state branches here when the weapon input bit is set.
The block selects the alternate player animation layout and weapon positioning table before Player_PrepareSpriteRendering_WithTables; no death or particle state is involved.
Holding the shot button in fixed-shooting mode diverts to the deceleration state before this test, which is what stops the player walking while aiming.
The acceleration is by facing rather than by the held direction, so this state is the one that turns the player and the weapon state is the one that does not.

The two halves agree: when the held direction matches bit 3 of $E the player enters the armed ground-weapon state, and when it does not it keeps the dash pose. The left half tests the same pair with the sense inverted.
The initializer assigns player state 0x04, whose handler validates lower-terrain contact and prepares the weapon sprite.
It does not check wall contact or initialize a wall-cling flag.
Both input guards of the weapon state share this return, and it sits at the end of the grounded movement init so the two states are contiguous in ROM.
The player state table maps state 0x04 to this routine, and Player_InitGroundWeaponState assigns that state.
The handler requires lower-terrain contact, prepares the weapon sprite, and accelerates horizontal movement; it is not an airborne state.
Mirror of the left-hand half: a direction that disagrees with the facing returns the player to the turning state, and one that agrees accelerates without turning.

State $56, which Player_StateHandlerOffsets resolves to Player_PhoenixAttackUpdate. It restricts the input mask to $73, spends both air-move flags, and installs $78000 of horizontal dash speed in $48 signed by the held direction or, with none held, by the current facing.
Left is tested first, so holding both directions dashes left.
Reached both from a held right and from the no-direction fallback when the player already faces right.
It installs the dash mapping and spawns the two trail objects, then returns 1 so the caller knows the move was taken.
A fresh C press while the attack runs resets the $50 counter to 7, which is the value the state below tests to decide whether to extend the dash.
When the $4E window expires the counter is rebuilt as 0 or 2 depending on whether $50 still equals 7, so a held button produces a longer follow-up dash.
The attack always ends in a dash attack: state $10 on the ground and state $24 while bit 4 of $E marks ceiling attachment, and Player_StateHandlerOffsets resolves both to Player_DashAttackState.
A non-zero PhoenixAttackStatus is the cooldown and bit 7 of PlayerRestrictionFlags is a stage-level block; either one suppresses the projectile.
SFX $A6 is the sound of a dash that produced no shot, and the same branch exists in the ordinary dash init.
Every frame of the attack sets bit 6 of $21 and bit 4 of $23, which are the hitbox-active and armour bits the collision pass reads, and runs both facing-selected terrain probes.
It calls the initialiser once, steps the pool pointer by one object and the table index by two, and then falls straight through into it a second time, so exactly two trails are built with no loop.

Each trail is a type-$10 object, Entity_NullUpdateHandler4, with its collision byte cleared, so it never updates and never collides; it inherits the player facing word and a draw priority four lower, clamped at zero.
The two table reads are four bytes apart with the same index, so the offset and the velocity of a trail are always taken as a pair.

Four words used as two interleaved pairs: offsets $20 and $FFE0 at indices 0 and 2, velocities $FFF8 and 8 at the same indices plus four. So the two trails start 32 pixels either side of the player and converge on it at 8 units a frame.
The ceiling entry point: it writes state $24 before joining the shared body, and the ground entry below writes $10. Both resolve to Player_DashAttackState.
Reached from the grounded Counter Force state and from the C-button handler, both of which are on the ground.
Field for field the same setup as Player_InitPhoenixAttack apart from the two counters: the dash clears $4E where the Phoenix attack sets it to 8.
The same left-first direction resolution the Phoenix attack uses.
Reached from a held right and from the facing fallback.
Both this branch and the blocked one below set PhoenixAttackStatus to $78 and return 1; they differ only in whether a projectile is spawned and which mapping is installed.
This is the branch taken when the cooldown or the restriction bit blocks the shot, so the former PlayDashAttackSound name described the exception as though it were the rule. SFX $A6 plays only here.
Both active dash state values 0x10 and 0x24 map to this routine in the player state table.
It updates repeated dash movement, terrain contact and the visual trail before performing cleanup only when the timer or collision ends the attack.
Both the external stop flag and the expiry of the $50 counter end the dash through the same facing-selected terrain probe.
It clears the same two collision bits the update sets each frame, and builds d0 as 0 or 1 so that the following test picks the floor or the ceiling contact bit by attachment.
The btst with a register index is what makes one instruction serve both the grounded and the ceiling case.
This is the site that identifies fall state $28 as the ceiling-detach variant: bit 4 of $E clear takes Player_InitFallState_Finish and set takes Player_InitCeilingDetachFall_Finish.
Its attachment test is inert: beq and bra both target Player_InitSlideState, so the branch is a two-instruction no-op and a dash that lands slides the same way on the ground and on the ceiling.
Here the same test is live: a grounded dash resumes through the crouch cleanup and a ceiling dash through the dash animation.
A one-instruction trampoline that exists because the three movement calls are too far from the cleanup for a short branch.
The movement helper is called three times in a row, so the dash advances three sub-steps a frame and stops at the first one that reports a wall.
It returns a collision only from the wall bits in 7(a5), chosen by the sign of $48; both screen clamps below return zero, so a dash stopped by the screen edge keeps running.
Bit 0 of 7(a5) is the left wall and bit 1 the right, selected by the sign of the dash velocity.
The clamps are skipped entirely while bit 1 of PlayerRestrictionFlags is set, which is how scripted sequences move the player outside the normal span.
The span is $90 to $1AF in screen coordinates, and the comparisons are word operations on the high half of the position long.
Both a clamped position and an unclamped one report no collision.
The only path that leaves with the flags set, which is the wall case the caller acts on.
State $40, which the table resolves to Player_HandleSlideState in two adjacent slots. The slide velocity is $20000 against the direction the dash was travelling, taken from the sign of $48.
It reuses $48, the dash velocity, as a two-frame animation counter once the sign has been consumed.
The same d0 trick as the dash cleanup picks the floor or ceiling contact bit, and losing that contact drops straight into the fall state.
Deceleration is $4000 a frame and the state ends the moment the velocity long reaches zero, not on a timer.
It renders through Player_RenderMotionPose, which is one of the five ground and ceiling callers that corrected that renderer from its former airborne name.

A bare return with zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in a branch so it cannot be fallen into. Its address comes from build/main.lst, because nullsub names carry a counter rather than an address.
State $44. It clears the ceiling attachment outright, so a dash kick always falls, and takes its direction from the sign of $48 like the slide.
The negative-velocity case skips the negate and returns here.
Gravity is the ordinary $8800 and landing halves the horizontal velocity after entering the slide, so a kick that lands slides at half the speed a dash does.
The airborne frames return here.

This is the C button handler for the two grounded states that call it. Without down held it jumps; with down held it dashes, unless a direction is also held or bit 6 of PlayerRestrictionFlags is set or the solid-terrain bit is clear, and the remaining case drops the player through the floor via Player_InitFallingTransition. The former name named none of those three outcomes.

This is the jump. It writes fall state $08, an upward $58000, and 5 into $48, which Player_HandleFallingState_UpdateJumpHold spends as the hold window in which gravity is suppressed. No other routine starts a jump from the ground.
Shared with Player_CheckDashInput, which is the ceiling counterpart of this handler.
The ceiling counterpart: C with up held dashes, C alone drops off the ceiling. It has no jump branch, because the ceiling states reach the air by detaching.
The ordinary fall entry, state $06, reached when a grounded state loses its floor contact.
The shared tail that callers with their own animation counter enter directly, and the exact routine Player_InitCeilingDetachFall_Finish mirrors with state $28.
The routine initializes fields consumed by UI_UpdateWeaponSelectionObject, including its animation counter and weapon-selection frame state.
Its object-table entry leads only to the weapon-selection update path and not to enemy targeting or combat logic.
The routine reads UI_WeaponSelectionSpriteFrames and calls UI_GetWeaponIconData and UI_ClearWeaponCounters.
Its input branches change the selected weapon, refill its value, clear UI counters, and refresh palette data; no boss target or combat state is accessed.
The entity dispatch-table entry performs one-time UI_InitWeaponSelectionObject setup and then tail-branches to UI_UpdateWeaponSelectionObject.
Both callees operate on weapon-selection display and input state, not boss initialization.
The routine selects pickup variant zero and enters the common initializer, which installs entity type 0x194 and the small health-restoration amount and sprite mapping.
It does not render a sprite or merely clear a register; its callers invoke it when combat objects are destroyed.
The routine selects pickup variant one before the common type-0x194 initializer.
Variant one uses the larger health-restoration amount, pickup sound, and pickup sprite mapping; no explosion controller is created.
The caller-provided mask is applied only to the random word to select the small or large pickup variant.
The routine is shared by ordinary enemies and projectiles and contains no Jetsripper attack state.
Entity type 0x194 is installed by the pickup initializer and maps to this update handler.
On collection the handler plays the pickup sound, adds 500 BCD score, increases PlayerHealth up to PlayerMaxHealth, and starts the transient value display.
The entry sets only the count exponent 3 and the mapping pointer before falling into the shared pattern routine, so the caller still supplies the speed shift in d1 and the start angle in d2.

The routine treats d0 as a power of two: it spawns exactly 2^d0 particles and divides the full $200 angle range by the same power, so the particles are always evenly spaced. The speed shift in d1 scales the sine and cosine pair.
Each iteration takes one free projectile slot, reads a sine and cosine pair at the running angle, and places the particle at the parent position.
A failed allocation skips the angle advance, so a short slot supply thins the ring rather than shifting it.
The variant A constructor allocates a type-$1A0 controller with six particle repetitions, picks one of four motion variants from two random bits, plays SFX $BB and shares the common initializer.
The variant B constructor is the same shape with type $1A4, eight repetitions and SFX $BC, and falls straight through into the common initializer.
Both constructors converge here to copy the parent position, install the flags and attribute word with the global priority bit, disable collision, and request shake level 2 on both planes.
Effect_SpawnExplosionA installs entity type 0x1A0, whose dispatch-table entry is this routine.
The handler bounds-checks the effect, manages its particle lifetime, and selects one of four random motion variants; it reads no enemy phase state.
Four self-relative words, but only three distinct handlers: variants 2 and 3 share the spiral dispatcher and differ only in whether the spiral restarts.
Variant 0 installs a fixed upward velocity on its first frame and then accelerates upward every frame after.
The repeat path subtracts a further $4000 from the vertical velocity each frame.
Variant 1 uses field $4E as a two-entry state index for its arc.
Two self-relative words: the launch away from the player and the gravity that follows it.
The launch takes the angle to the player, adds half a turn so the motion is away from the player, and converts that direction into the initial velocity.
Every later frame of the arc adds $4000 to the vertical velocity.
Variants 2 and 3 both enter here and use field $4E as a three-entry state index.
Three self-relative words: seed the angle, convert it to velocity, and advance the spiral.
The first spiral state seeds the angle from the random state and falls through into the conversion, so both state advances happen on the same frame.
The conversion scales the sine and cosine pair by sixteen into both velocity fields and arms a four-frame step timer.
Each time the step timer expires the angle is turned back by $40 and the state returns to the conversion, which is what makes the path spiral rather than travel straight.
Variant 3 alone clears the spiral state entirely, so it reseeds a fresh random angle instead of continuing the turn.
Independently of the motion variant, the controller runs a three-state particle loop keyed on field 4.
Three self-relative words: spawn one particle, wait, and finally remove the controller.
One particle is placed at the controller's position and a four-frame gap is armed.
When the gap expires the repetition counter in $4A is spent and the state steps back to the spawner, so the controller emits its six particles four frames apart.
The exhausted counter advances instead to the removal state.
Both variants share this single instruction, which sets the removal bit that the visible-object pass acts on.
Effect_SpawnExplosionB installs entity type 0x1A4, whose dispatch-table entry is this routine.
Its random selector dispatches only particle-loop and radial-ring explosion patterns, not boss-part states.
Four self-relative words: the repeating particle loop and the three ring patterns.
The only parent dispatch is explosion B's variant table, and the child states spawn common explosion particles around the controller.
No Snake boss state, Snake-specific mapping, or projectile attack parameters are referenced.
Three self-relative words mirroring variant A's lifetime states.
Variant B's loop scatters each particle inside a 64-pixel box centred on the controller and arms a two-frame gap, half of variant A's.
The counter is tested with a signed branch rather than a zero test, so variant B emits one more particle than its counter value suggests.
The exhausted counter advances to the removal state.

The pattern fires once on the controller's first frame and calls the radial spawner three times with exponent 1, so each ring is two particles, at speed shifts 1, 3 and 5 from one shared random start angle.
Two calls with exponent 2 give four particles each at speed shifts 3 and 5, and the second ring is rotated by $40 so the two do not overlap.
One call with exponent 3 gives a single eight-particle ring at speed shift 4.
Boss_BugmaxSpawnDebris initializes entity type 0x348 with a lifetime, rectangular spread dimensions, and randomized initial delay.
This handler repeatedly creates particles inside that rectangle and waits between them, so it is a debris spawner rather than Bugmax's main projectile controller.
The main gameplay loop calls the routine unconditionally in its stage-effects chain, and the routine dispatches only the global state stored at 0xFF8114.
Its active path allocates an enemy object, searches terrain near the player, and installs entity type 0x1C; it neither identifies Jetsripper nor moves an existing boss.
Three words measured from EnemySpawn_ResetDirectorState rather than absolute addresses; state 0 is a bare return, so the director is idle until something sets its state word.
The reset clears the director state and falls straight into the shared return.
The paused-game path, the idle state, the running timer and every failed allocation share this single return.
State 2 advances to the running state and arms a fixed $A0-frame first delay, after which every later delay is randomized.
On expiry the director picks a new delay, allocates a slot, chooses a search origin, sets a random one-bit search pass, and on success stamps the new record as type $1C.

No direct caller occurs in reconstructed source and its absolute address is absent from the ROM pointer scan, although two neighboring entry points are found there. This makes the routine orphaned in the static graph, not proven impossible to invoke indirectly; its instructions clear EnemySpawnDelayTimer and three otherwise unused longwords.
Each later delay is a random value between $20 and $9F frames.

The search normally starts at Y $1D0, but above the default difficulty, with the camera nearly still and the player past X $C0, one draw in four starts at $70 instead, which is what lets enemies appear from above.
All four rejection tests converge on the default origin and return here.
The routine scans four 0x60-byte object records for a zero type field and clears the selected record.
It returns failure when every slot is occupied and does not read or write animation-frame data.
Only four records are available to this director, scanned from the twenty-second entity slot.
The chosen record is cleared through the shared block clear, which advances the pointer, so the routine steps it back by one record before returning.
The routine converts player-relative coordinates to layout offsets and scans collision-layout bytes for a consecutive open run.
Its success result supplies the position written into a newly allocated enemy object; no attack timer is updated.
Each of the twenty-four rows tests two horizontal probes against the terrain collision buffer and treats a row as clear only when either probe reports empty.
A candidate needs seven consecutive clear rows, and the random search pass then decides whether the first such run is taken or skipped in favour of the next.
Each step moves eight pixels up and one layout row back, with both offsets masked to the layout's wrap.
Success returns zero in d7 while an exhausted search returns one, which is the convention the caller tests.
The helper converts a camera-relative coordinate pair into a byte offset into the terrain layout, masking the horizontal part to $7E and the vertical part to $1F80.
The chosen position is stored $20 pixels above the found row, and a spawn left of the midpoint additionally sets bit 7 of field $5F.
Right-side spawns return here without setting that flag.
The shared Enemy_MainStateMachine and delayed-destruction handler call this routine for entity type 0x1C.
It applies variant parameters from a local four-byte table and contains no boss-specific state or mapping.
Both facings converge here; the flag set at spawn time is what clears the horizontal flip bit for left-side enemies before this point.
One three-byte record; only index zero is ever passed, and the third byte is scaled by sixteen into field $5A.
The animation request in $5C is biased by four before indexing, so a request of zero means no change.
States that requested no animation return here.
Acceleration is applied in the facing direction and clamped at $20000 in either sign.
The rightward branch below the limit adds the acceleration step.
The left-facing entry repeats the same clamp against the negative limit.
The leftward branch below the limit subtracts the acceleration step.
Deceleration uses asymmetric steps: $3800 toward zero from the positive side and a $FFFFC800 threshold on the negative side.
An already stationary enemy and the completed positive step share this return.
The negative branch adds the same step back toward zero.
Both signs snap to exactly zero once the remaining speed is inside one step.
The spawner returns without firing when no projectile slot is free.
The muzzle offset and the launch angle are both mirrored by the facing bit, and the shot takes the enemy's draw bucket minus four so it renders in front.
The shot speed is derived from DifficultyMode halved plus nine, so the difficulty changes the projectile speed rather than the firing rate.
Enemy_BehaviorController enters this routine when the enemy is defeated or leaves its active conditions.
The routine converts the current object to entity type 0x1D4, assigns falling velocity and defeat animation data, and spawns no projectile pattern.
The right-facing case keeps the default negative horizontal velocity and returns here.
Entity type 0x1D4 maps to this handler, which applies gravity, blinks, and counts down one object.
At expiry it creates one explosion and either removes the object or converts it to a randomly sized resource pickup; it does not spawn multiple shots.
The counting frames return here; the last one retypes the object to $1C, which is index 7 and therefore the shared behaviour controller.
It reads StandardEnemyTileAttr, a stage variable, so the same routine gives different art per stage, and installs $2A of health.
The request in $5C is indexed less four, so the three legal requests are 4, 8 and $C, exactly the values the four periodic-shot states write.
A zero request leaves the current animation in place.
Index $11 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, which is type $44. An object whose collision byte is zero skips the defeat test entirely, and a defeated one explodes and drops a type-3 pickup.
Both the no-collision path and the surviving path converge here.
Four self-relative words measured from Enemy_InitializeWithHealth.
Four entries forming a loop: the last state returns to the second, so the enemy alternates between waiting and shooting for as long as it lives.
Health $62, the highest in this module, against the $2A the shared sprite setup installs for the behaviour enemies.
The loop re-entry point, reached from the periodic-shot state when its window expires.
State 2 waits out whatever $48 holds and then arms $28 frames with animation 8.
The enemy wait returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; expiry advances state and seeds $48=$28 and $5C=8.
State 4 arms the long $180-frame shooting window with animation $C.
The timed enemy state returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; expiry advances state and seeds $48=$180 and $5C=$C.
State 6. When the window expires it arms $120 frames and jumps back to the wait entry rather than advancing.
A shot is fired whenever the low five bits of the counter are zero, so the $180-frame window produces twelve shots.
The frames between shots return here.
The projectile counterpart of the enemy sprite setup, reading EnemyProjectileTileAttr and installing $F of health and a $08 armour byte.
Shared by the projectile attack and homing attack controllers in the neighbouring module.
A zero request leaves the current animation in place.
Ten long pointers, the largest animation table in the module, covering requests 4 through $28.
A fixed $30000 either way, chosen by bit 3 of $E, so the caller does not have to negate anything itself.
The leftward case is $FFFD0000, which is the same magnitude negated.
The step is $4000 a frame and the routine stops exactly at zero rather than oscillating, because a value already inside one step is cleared.
A zero velocity and a completed positive step share this return.
The negative half tests against $FFFFC000, the negated step, for the same reason.
Both halves clear the velocity outright when it is within one step of zero.
The angle is rounded by adding $20 before the shift, so each of the eight sectors is centred on its direction rather than starting at it.

Bit 0 of the table pointer is a flip flag rather than part of the address: the routine clears it with bclr, sets the sprite flip bit when it was set, and stores the cleaned pointer. Four of the eight table entries carry the $1.
Eight long pointers over six distinct animations, four of them with 1 added to carry the flip flag, so the table encodes both the frame and the mirroring in one long.
Eight signed byte pairs indexed by the same sector halved, giving the muzzle offset for each of the eight directions.
Enemy_HomingAttackController enters this routine when its current object is defeated.
The routine converts that object to entity type 0x1D8, assigns falling velocity and an alternate defeat mapping, and accesses no Jetsripper idle state.
The right-facing case keeps the default negative horizontal velocity, so the debris is always thrown backwards relative to the facing.
Entity type 0x1D8 maps to this handler after the shared homing-attack enemy is defeated.
It applies gravity and blinking, then creates an explosion and resource pickup; no Jetsripper-specific data is referenced.
The visibility bit is toggled from bit 0 of the timer's low byte, the same blink the beetle, wasp and shared defeat objects use.

For a nonexpired $48 timer, the alternate defeat projectile sets object bit 7, retains it when $49 bit zero is set, or clears it before this RTS otherwise; expiration takes the explosion and pickup path with random mask 7.
The dispatch table covers an enemy's idle, approach, airborne, defeat, and ground-attack states.
The controller uses terrain collision, faces the player, and only spawns a projectile during one timed ground state; the controlled object is not itself a projectile.
The controller runs the state and then the shared projectile animation update, so each state only has to request an animation in $5C.
The dispatcher clears the animation request and indexes seven words measured from Enemy_ProjectileAttackInit rather than absolute addresses.
Seven entries over six distinct handlers: states 6 and 8 both resolve to the airborne handler and differ only in the animation the entry that set them requested, $28 for a fall and $24 for a leap.
State 0 installs 30 units of health and the shared projectile sprite, then falls into the idle entry.
The idle entry arms a $60-frame hold and clears the horizontal velocity; both the init and the landing path reach it.
Losing ground contact sends the enemy airborne at any point. Otherwise, once the hold expires it faces the player and attacks when the distance is under $60 or approaches when it is not.
The timer is re-tested after the facing update because Enemy_FacePlayer does not preserve it.
Every frame of the hold tail-calls the shared horizontal friction, so the enemy coasts to a stop rather than stopping instantly.
The approach is state 4 with animation 8.
The approach returns to idle once the player is within $50, which is closer than the $60 the idle state uses to start an attack, so the two thresholds leave a deliberate gap.
Either wall-contact bit in field 7 converts the approach into a leap, which is state 8 with an upward $FFFA4000 velocity.
Two airborne entries in Enemy_ProjectileAttackStateOffsets target this routine.
It applies capped gravity and checks upper and lower terrain for the shared enemy object; no boss identity is tested.
Gravity is $6000 per frame and the fall is capped at $7C000.
The floor probe runs only while descending, and a contact returns the enemy to the idle entry.
The ceiling probe is the tail call of the airborne state, so it runs on every rising frame.
Entering the air halves the horizontal velocity, which is why a leap carries further than a walk-off.
The attack is state $C with a $36-frame window.
The single shot is fired on the one frame the counter equals $1E, halfway through the window, with the muzzle offset and velocity mirrored by the facing bit.
Both facings converge on the type-$1D0 trailing-arc hazard spawner.
The enemy stops tracking the player once fewer than $10 frames remain, so it commits to its final facing before the window closes.
The last $10 frames return here without a facing update.
Enemy_ProjectileAttackController calls the routine only after its health field becomes negative.
The routine clears collision fields, assigns defeat animation and velocity, then enters the shared explosion-and-pickup fall state; it has no Joker attack behavior.
State $A is reached both by falling through the converter above and by the state table, so the conversion and the state share one entry.
The same timer-driven blink the alternate defeat projectile uses.

The defeat-fall state reaches this RTS from both $49-bit-zero outcomes after setting object bit 7 and optionally clearing it; an expired $48 timer instead explodes and enters the pickup path with random mask 7.

Two words indexed by DifficultyMode used directly as a byte offset, giving a $98-frame delay at difficulty 0 and $60 at difficulty 2. The word read and the direct index make this difficulty scaling work, unlike the byte-tested pattern in the weapon ammo costs.
The companion table, indexed the same way, giving one shot at difficulty 0 and four at difficulty 2.
Its state table initializes an enemy, waits a difficulty-indexed delay, and emits a difficulty-indexed number of tracked projectiles.
The object has its own health and defeat conversion, so it is the homing-attack enemy controller rather than an alternative projectile.
The same state-then-animation shape as the projectile attack controller.
Three words measured from Enemy_HomingAttackInit.
Init, wait and burst; the burst returns to the wait rather than to the init, so the delay table is consulted on every cycle.
Ten units of health and the shared projectile sprite, then the wait entry.
The wait entry reads the difficulty-scaled delay, and the burst state branches back here when its shot count runs out.
A bare countdown with no movement or probing.
The burst entry seeds the animation counter at $80 and reads the difficulty-scaled shot count.
Shots are emitted only while the animation counter stays at or above $80, so the burst is paced by the animation rather than by a separate timer.
The off-animation frames and a full projectile pool share this return.
The object uses the same sprite setup, animation update, health field, and defeat-object conversion as the adjacent ordinary enemy families.
Its two states only initialize and repeat an idle animation timer; no boss health, phase, or boss-only dispatch is present.
This controller uses the behaviour animation update rather than the projectile one, which is the only structural difference from the two above it.
Two words measured from Enemy_ShipPatrolInit.
The shortest state table in the module: an init and a single idle state.
The init uses the shared behaviour sprite setup rather than the projectile one, matching its animation update.
The state only re-requests animation $10 every $38 frames; it never moves the object, so its motion comes from elsewhere.
The frames between requests return here.
All callers operate on the current enemy object in a5.
The routine performs the shared entity wall check and lower-terrain check and never references the player object or player state.
The routine initializes object display flags, sprite priority, collision dimensions, and an animation-state timer for the adjacent phase enemy.
It writes no VDP port or VDP command buffer; the alleged VDP flag is the object's display-flags word.

Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs this handler. Before dispatching it retires the object through Enemy_ResetPhasePattern when its health goes negative or the stage spawn countdown expires, and steps the random generator once per frame.
The surviving path runs the state dispatcher and then the shared animation selector.
The dispatcher clears the animation request in $5C so each state must set it again, then indexes the seven self-relative words of Enemy_PhasePatternStateOffsets.
Seven self-relative words naming the init, wait, airborne, pre-attack, drift-start, drift-stop and restart states.
State 0 installs the sprite through the shared setup helper, requests animation 4, arms a $100-frame wait and advances, falling straight into the wait state.

The wait state leaps early when bit 5 of ControllerPressedState is pressed, giving the object an upward velocity of $FFFA0000 unless it is already inverted, so the enemy reacts to the player's own input rather than to a timer alone.
The no-input and already-inverted paths share this return.
When the wait expires without input the state skips the airborne phase entirely and jumps to the drift-start state with animation $10.
The phase-pattern state table targets this routine as one complete object state, not as a general trajectory helper.
It applies capped gravity, probes upper or lower terrain according to vertical direction, aligns the object to the contacted surface, and returns to the wait state.
The airborne state caps the fall at $80000 and then chooses a downward $20 probe or an upward $FFE4 probe from the sign of the current vertical velocity.
The rising branch supplies the negative probe offset so ceilings are tested on the way up.
Both probes converge here; a contact returns the object to the waiting state, shakes both planes, and aligns it to whichever surface it met.
The ceiling contact sets the vertical flip bit and aligns to the terrain top, which is how the enemy ends up hanging upside down.
A probe that found nothing returns here with the object still airborne.
A $20-frame hold that ends by requesting animation $14.
The frames before that timer expires return here.
After another $20 frames the state installs a one-unit leftward velocity and animation $1C.
The frames before that timer expires return here.
The drift is cleared after $20 more frames and animation $18 is requested.
The frames before that timer expires return here.
The final state rearms the $100-frame wait, requests animation 4 again, and returns the object to the waiting state, closing the cycle.
The frames before that timer expires return here.
The retirement path rewrites the object's type to $290, clears its state, health, both collision bytes and its velocity, and arms a $40-frame timer, so the record is recycled rather than removed.
Entity type 0x294 applies gravity and terrain alignment while allocating randomized type-0x88 child particles.
When its lifetime expires it creates an explosion and resource pickup, so the object is a defeat-debris spawner rather than an ordinary projectile.

Two families share this setup, the circling enemy and the Stage 9 fly. It merges the shared tile attribute with the global priority bit and reads three bytes from Enemy_CirclingSpriteParameters at the caller's index, the last of which is scaled by sixteen into field $5A.
Two three-byte records packed into four words, one per family, holding the bytes the setup helper distributes into fields $27, $25 and $5A.
The controller tail-calls this after each state. It does nothing unless the state requested an animation in $5C, and the request is biased by four before indexing.
States that requested no animation return here, which is the usual case since the dispatcher clears $5C every frame.
A single long pointer; only the approach state requests an animation, and it requests index four, which the bias turns into this one entry.
The orbit and exit states use this to pick both a mapping and a sprite attribute word from the current angle, rounding it to sixteen sectors and then halving the index for the attribute table.
Sixteen long pointers over only five distinct mappings, mirrored about the two half-turns, so the sprite is reused with flips rather than drawn for every angle.
Sixteen words supplying the flip bits that complete the mirroring, which is why the mapping table can repeat.

The helper reads a sine and cosine pair for the current angle, scales them by the caller's d2 and d3 into the velocity fields, and every 128 frames, staggered per object by adding the record address, fires one aimed two-speed shot if the player is at least $20 away.
The off-phase frames, the too-close case and the no-free-slot case share this return.
Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs this handler. It retires the object through Enemy_ResetCirclingState on negative health, on bit 7 of the contact byte, or when the stage spawn countdown expires.
The surviving path runs the state dispatcher and then the animation update.
The dispatcher clears the animation request and indexes the five self-relative words of Enemy_CirclingStateOffsets.
Five self-relative words naming the approach, distance-check, orbit, exit and terminal no-op states.
State 0 installs the sprite with family index zero, requests animation four, seeds a randomized approach velocity and advances, falling into the distance check.
The approach continues steering until the player is within $60 horizontally.
Entering the orbit seeds angle $180, rotation step $10, a $10-frame step timer and a $100-frame lifetime.
The helper stores the camera-absolute spawn point in $52 and $54 as the steering target and takes an eight-times-scaled sine and cosine pair at a random angle as the initial velocity.
The routine compares the current circling enemy position with stored target coordinates plus random jitter and adjusts its two velocity components.
It neither scans nor clears the enemy pool and performs no stage-number check.
The rightward branch accelerates by $4000 per frame and clamps at $20000, mirroring the leftward branch's $FFFE0000 limit.
Both horizontal outcomes converge here to repeat the same acceleration and clamping on the vertical axis, against a separately randomized target offset.
Control reaches this branch when target Y minus current Y is positive.
It adds 0x4000 to vertical velocity and caps it at positive 0x20000, which is downward in the game's screen-coordinate convention rather than upward.

Index $AA of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, which is type $2A8, the value Stage9_FlyFormationActivateWaveState writes into each staged slot. State zero is exempt from the defeat checks, the same shape the Stage 12 enemies use.
The state runs first and the shared circling animation second.
Three self-relative words measured from the table itself.
Three entries. Unlike the Stage 12 tables every slot is reachable: the orbit state advances to slot 2 once its phase counter reaches 8.

It seeds the orbit at angle $180 with target $80 and scale $10, then reads $58 to pick the direction. $58 is written by the formation controller from its wave counter, so wave 0 orbits with a positive step of 8 and wave 1 with $FFF8.
The reverse branch differs only in the sign of the angular step; both fall into the orbit state on the same frame.
The angle in $4C is stepped by $4A and masked to $1FF, so the circle is 512 units. The state only consults the phase tables on the exact frame the angle equals the target in $4E.
The same three loads from the mirrored tables, chosen on $58 again rather than on the sign of the current step.
The phase counter $48 steps by two and the state ends at 8, which is one phase after the last table entry.
Both the frames short of the target angle and the frames short of the final phase return here.

Three words, and the phase counter reaches 6 before the state checks for 8, so the table is read one entry past its end on the final phase. At offset 6 it reads the first word of Enemy_Stage9FlyForwardTargetAngles, $100. The value is stored into $4A and never used, because the same frame moves the fly to its no-op state.
Three words, read the same way, so the fourth read takes $10 from the first word of the speed table below.
Three words; the fourth read takes $FFFE from the first word of the reverse step table.
The mirror of the forward step table, negated. The overrun on the reverse side is the same shape.
Three words. Its own overrun reads $10 from the reverse speed table.

Three words, and the last table of the group, so its overrun reads the two bytes that follow it: the $4E75 return opcode of Enemy_Stage9FlyNoOpState. That value lands in the speed scale of a fly that is about to stop updating, which is why nothing shows.

Slot 2 of the fly table, and genuinely entered: the orbit state writes the $CF00 sprite word and advances into it once the phase counter reaches 8, so a finished fly sits here inert while the controller keeps animating it. Its address comes from build/main.lst, because nullsub names carry a counter rather than an address.
Projectile_InitViblackSideShot installs entity type 0x2F4, whose dispatch-table entry is this controller, and the only initializer call comes from Viblack's attack code.
Its states enter from a screen side, rotate, launch horizontally, track Viblack's stored altitude, and end in a projectile burst; no walker movement or Stage 17 discriminator is present.
It shares Enemy_UpdateCirclingAnimation with the fly, which is why the two objects of this module draw from the same animation helper.
Five self-relative words, and it clears the animation request first like the fly dispatcher.
Five entries covering init, approach, begin turn, turn and launch, and track. The routine that sits in the source between the approach and the begin turn is not in this table at all.
It compares the player centre X against its own X and stores $FFF8 or 8 into $4E, so the turn direction is chosen once, at birth, from which side the player is on.
The branch taken when the player is to the left.
The test is against PlayerCenterY, not against any boss field: the state waits until the shot sits between $20 and $7FFF below the player centre. The comment that named a stored Viblack Y was wrong.

Zero references of any kind: no table slot, no branch, no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in rts so it cannot be fallen into. It is the only reader of $4A in the side-shot object, and the sequence controller still copies its own $4A into every child it spawns, so the link field is written by live code and read by nothing. That is what identifies this as a cut state rather than a helper.
Live through the approach state, which branches here twice, and also used by the orphaned routine above.
It stops the entry descent and arms a $10-frame turn.

The launch sign is taken from bit 7 of the high byte of $4E, which is set only for the $FFF8 turn, so the shot leaves toward the side the player was on when it was born: three pixels a frame, and a $1C0-frame lifetime.
Both the turning frames and the negative-turn launch return here.
When the lifetime runs out it sets bit 4 of the sprite flag byte, the same hide flag the Stage 12 objects use, rather than freeing the slot.
The frames still within the lifetime return here.

It reads PlayerCenterY and accelerates $2000 a frame toward it, capped at $20000 either way, which is two pixels a frame. The former name attributed this to a boss altitude; no boss field is read anywhere in the routine.
The downward half of the same symmetric acceleration.
Exact alignment with the player centre, and both capped cases, return here.
Reached from the controller on defeat, on the collision bit, or on the stage countdown. It clears the combat fields and tail-jumps into the shared quad-projectile spawner.
A bare return with zero references of any kind, and the routine above it ends in a tail jump, so it cannot be fallen into either. Its address comes from build/main.lst.
Stage9_InitializeFlyCorridor installs entity type 0x2AC, whose dispatch-table entry is this routine.
The state machine allocates four dormant object slots and activates them one by one as type-0x2A8 Stage 9 flies; it controls the formation rather than moving one fly.
Four entries. The activate state writes 4 rather than advancing when the first wave finishes, so the allocate and activate pair runs twice.
The controller parks itself at $120, $90 and arms a $20-frame delay. That position is the centre both waves are offset from.
It clears $4A, the wave counter, only on the first pass, because the activate state sets it to 1 and then re-enters at the allocate state rather than here.
The Stage 9 formation delay returns here while timer $48 is nonzero; expiry clears field $4A and advances controller state.

The counter runs from 0 to $10 in steps of two and the slots are stored from $4C upward, so it reserves eight objects, not four as the comment claimed. Each is parked at type $10, Entity_NullUpdateHandler4, until the wave activates it.
A full object pool and the frames before the eighth slot share this return, so allocation simply retries.
This formation-controller state walks the stored slot array and converts one dormant slot to type 0x2A8 at fixed intervals.
After the first four entries it restarts from the alternate horizontal offset, and only hides the controller after both waves; it is not a fly death handler.
Wave 0 is pushed $100 to the right of the controller and wave 1 $80 to the left, so the two waves enter from opposite sides.
Fifteen frames in sixteen return here, because the release is gated on the frame counter rather than on a timer of its own.
The first completion sets the wave counter to 1 and sends the state back to the allocate slot; the second falls through to the finish.
The controller hides itself with the same bit-4 flag its children use.
Boss_ViblackSpawnSideShot is the only direct caller and supplies an alternating left/right horizontal position.
The routine installs entity type 0x2F4, which dispatches to Projectile_ViblackSideShotController; it has no walker owner.
The routine is called from Viblack's active attack and defeat-check paths and alternates the spawned object's horizontal position between two screen sides.
It tail-calls Projectile_InitViblackSideShot, whose type-0x2F4 state machine contains no walker behavior.

Its one caller passes d0 as zero, so only the first parameter record is ever read. The sprite attribute word comes from BirdEnemyTileAttr, a stage variable, which is how the same enemy takes different art in different stages.
One four-byte record read as three bytes: $18 into $27, 6 into $25, and $11 shifted left four into $5A. The 6 is the health, and Enemy_BirdInit overwrites it with 2 when the yacht is present.
The request in $5C is indexed less four, so the four legal requests are 4, 8, $C and $10, which are exactly the values the bird states write.
A zero request leaves the current mapping alone, which is why the dispatcher can clear $5C every frame.
Four long pointers covering the four requests.

Shared with Enemy_Stage10WaspController. The bit-7 test is a byte operation on the top byte of the $18 velocity long, so it is a sign test, and a zero velocity leaves the flip bit untouched rather than resetting it.
Bit 11 of the sprite attribute word is the horizontal flip, set for leftward motion and cleared for rightward.
Both the zero-velocity case and the flip-setting case return here.

Index $24 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, which is type $90, the value the Stage 12 turret writes when it spawns a bird. State zero is exempt from the defeat checks, and unlike the Stage 12 controllers this one has a fourth exit: with bit 7 of $22 set and bit 4 clear it plays SFX $BC and retypes itself to a type-$88 effect on the spot.
The random state is advanced once per frame per bird, which is what feeds the tracking jitter below.
Three steps rather than the two the Stage 12 controllers use: state, animation, then the shared velocity-driven flip.
Fourteen self-relative words measured from the table itself.

Fourteen entries, states $00 to $1A, and every one is a distinct handler. The bird advances by 2, by 4, by 6 and by 8 at different points and also steps backwards by 2 and by 4, so unlike the Stage 12 enemies its state graph is not a straight line.

A bare return with zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match. It sits immediately after the state table, which is data, so nothing can fall into it either, and the fourteen table slots all name other handlers. Its address comes from build/main.lst.
Bit 0 of $5F selects the spawn edge, X $1E0 on the right with the flip bit set or X $70 on the left with it clear, so the spawner picks the side by setting one bit.
The left edge is $70 against the right edge $1E0, and the flip bit is cleared to match.

Bit 1 of $5F sends the bird straight to the wait state instead of the entry state. On the entry path it then tests whether the object in the Entity57 slot is type $1B8, Stage12_YachtControllerMain, and if so lowers the health from the table value 6 to 2. Birds in the yacht stage take a third of the damage to kill.
State 6 is the wait, reached directly from the init when bit 1 of $5F is set.
The non-yacht entry path returns here without touching the health.
The state writes only the horizontal velocity field at offset 0x18, choosing negative or positive 0x20000 from the spawn-side flag.
It does not change vertical velocity or perform terrain checks; the later Enemy_BirdDiveAttack state owns that behavior.
The entry velocity is $20000 rightward or $20000 leftward, selected by the same bit 0 of $5F that chose the spawn edge, so a bird always flies away from the edge it entered on.
A bsr followed by rts where a bra would do, so the state is a pure wrapper around the shot spawner and never advances the state itself.
It arms $4A with 4, which is the number of wait-and-chase cycles the bird will run before the chase state gives up and starts the long attack.

Zero references of any kind and no ROM absolute-address match, and the routine above it ends in rts so it cannot be fallen into. Its two instructions are the wall check and the lower terrain probe that Enemy_BirdDiveAttack performs inline with other work between them, so it reads as a helper that was inlined and left behind.
It caches the wall-contact byte 7(a5) into $58 every frame, and the chase state later reads that cached byte to decide how steeply to climb.
The floor probe runs only while descending, but the ceiling probe runs on every frame, so a rising bird is stopped by a ceiling and an ascending one ignores the floor.
Reaching terminal velocity $58000 without touching ground skips four states forward, straight to the upward acceleration.
A floor contact clears the horizontal velocity and arms a four-frame wait, so a landed bird pauses before its next move.
Two nested counters: $48 counts frames and $4A counts how many wait-and-chase cycles remain out of the 4 the dive setup armed.
The frames inside one wait return here.
When the cycle counter runs out the bird skips forward by 4 with a $40-frame timer rather than by the usual 2.
A horizontal distance under $80 sends the bird up at $58000 and forward six states; further away it steps back four states and climbs more gently.
The chase speed is the same $20000 the entry uses, only the sign differs.
The $80 threshold is the only distance test in the whole bird state machine.
The cached wall byte from the dive decides between two climb rates, so a bird that hit a wall on its dive climbs at $50000 and one that did not at $28000.
The shallow climb also requests animation $10, the only state that uses the fourth mapping.
Both climb rates return here.
It re-arms the cycle counter to 4 and steps back two states, which is what makes the wait-and-chase pair a loop.
The bird wait returns here while timer $48 is nonnegative; expiry sets field $4A to four and subtracts two from controller state.
The state subtracts 0x4000 from vertical velocity until reaching negative 0x58000.
Negative vertical velocity moves upward in the engine's downward-positive screen-coordinate convention, so the old descend claim was reversed.
The state accelerates by $4000 a frame until the velocity passes $58000 upward, the same magnitude the dive uses downward.
Its threshold is $28000, under half the upward one, so the bird falls back more slowly than it climbs.
The bird state returns here while vertical velocity remains below $28000 after a $4000 increment; on reaching the threshold it advances object state by two before the same RTS.
The state repeatedly subtracts 0x4000 from vertical velocity until it reaches negative 0x20000.
It therefore continues through zero into upward motion before starting the attack timer, rather than merely decelerating downward.
The reversal ends at only $20000 upward and then arms the $100-frame attack window.
The longest state at $100 frames, and the only one that runs both the tracking helper and the shot spawner every frame.
The frames inside the attack window return here.
The state adds 0x4000 to vertical velocity until reaching positive 0x20000.
Positive vertical velocity is downward in screen coordinates, contradicting the generated ascend description.
The exit threshold is $20000, the gentlest of the three acceleration states.

The last state and the only one with no exit: it pushes the vertical velocity upward while it is positive and the horizontal one away from zero, so a bird that reaches it drifts off screen and is collected by the spawn countdown.
Both halves test bit 7 of the top byte of a velocity long, the same sign test the flip helper uses.
The horizontal step is $800 against the vertical $2000, so the drift is mostly upward.

The aim point is re-randomised only on frames where the low five bits of the frame counter are zero, so the offsets in $4C and $4E hold for $20 frames at a time and the bird weaves rather than homing.
The target is the player centre plus the jitter, with a fixed $60 subtracted from the vertical, so the bird aims above the player rather than at it.
The horizontal acceleration is $2000 a frame, clamped at $20000.
Reached from four places, including the exact-alignment cases of the horizontal half.
The vertical acceleration is $4000 a frame, twice the horizontal, with the same $20000 clamp.
Exact vertical alignment and both clamped cases share this return.

It fires on one frame in $20 and, unlike every other spawner in this module, does not test the result of Projectile_FindFreeSlotForward before writing, so a full pool is overwritten rather than skipped.
The shot leaves $10 pixels to the side the bird is facing, with the muzzle offset and the velocity sign taken from the same bit.
The off-interval frames return here.
It retypes to $1DC, index $77 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable, and negates the horizontal velocity so the debris is thrown back the way the bird came.
Enemy_ConvertBirdToDefeatDebris changes a defeated bird to entity type 0x1DC, whose dispatch-table entry is this routine.
The handler applies gravity, emits visual particles, creates a radial destruction effect and either spawns a pickup or removes the debris; it does not create the bird's attack projectile.
A particle is spawned on one frame in eight, and $4A counts those particles down from 4, so the debris lasts $20 frames before it bursts.

The same test and the same response as Enemy_UpdateStage12DefeatDebris_HideInsteadOfPickup: while the object in the Entity57 slot is type $1B8, the yacht, the debris sets bit 4 of its sprite flag byte and drops nothing. The former name spoke of a special stage without naming the condition or the effect.
The off-interval frames, a full object pool and the counting frames all share this return.
Enemy_BirdSpawnShot installs entity type 0x2BC, whose dispatch-table entry is this controller, outside any Stage 10-specific constructor.
Its two states initialize generic projectile collision fields and apply gravity, impact, bounds and lifetime handling; no fly AI or Stage 10 state is read.
Two self-relative words; the init state falls straight into the update, so the table's second entry is only used from the second frame onward.
This first state initializes display, collision and damage fields on the type-0x2BC falling shot before entering Projectile_FallingShotUpdate.
It selects no fly animation, movement state or Stage 10 object data.

The shot accelerates downward and stops on either of the two collision bits in field $22. While the shared entity slot holds type $1B8 it uses that object's own position as its bounds instead of the terrain buffer, which is the special-stage variant of the same shot.
In the special-stage variant the shot is converted once it passes Y $150 rather than on terrain contact.
The ordinary variant probes the terrain buffer directly beneath itself.
All three impact paths clear both velocities, install a $C8-frame lifetime, and tail-call the shared explosion initializer.
A shot still in flight returns here from either bounds test.
The setup follows the same shape as the beetle and circling-enemy setups, reading three bytes from its own parameter record and scaling the last by sixteen into field $5A.
One three-byte record; only index zero is ever passed.
The animation request in $5C is biased by four before indexing, and the dispatcher clears it every frame, so a state that requests nothing keeps its current animation.
States that requested no animation return here.
Four long pointers matching the four requests the states make: $4, $8, $C and $10.

Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs this handler. It has three retirement paths rather than one: negative health and an expired stage spawn countdown both convert the wasp to falling debris, while bit 7 of the contact byte turns it into the shared type-$88 effect instead, unless bit 4 is also set.
A live wasp steps the random generator once per frame and clears its contact flags before the state runs.
The state, the animation and the facing update run in that order, with the facing taken from the sign of the horizontal velocity.
The dispatcher clears the animation request and indexes the six self-relative words of Enemy_Stage10WaspStateOffsets.
Six self-relative words naming the init, flight, wait, prepare-attack, dive and cooldown states.
The first state seeds both loop counters at three, requests animation $C, and places the wasp at X $1E0 or $70 according to bit 0 of field $5F.
The left-edge variant is selected by the spawn flag rather than by the player's position.
Flight checks walls every frame, tests the floor only while descending, and tests the ceiling only while rising, so each probe runs in the half of the arc where it can matter.
The rising and no-contact paths converge on the ceiling probe and one gravity step.
A floor contact stops the horizontal drift, requests animation $10, and arms a ten-frame wait.
The wait is the loop head: while the outer counter is still positive it spends one inner repetition, and an exhausted inner counter diverts to the cooldown instead of the attack.
Both the exhausted-outer-loop case and a surviving inner repetition advance into the attack preparation.
The frames before the wait expires return here.
Entering the cooldown skips three state slots at once, requesting animation 4 and a $20-frame pause.
A one-frame state that requests animation 8 and arms the ten-frame dive delay.

The dive returns the wasp to the flight state and picks its horizontal direction from the player's side, but negates that direction while the outer counter is zero, so the final pass of the cycle dives away from the player rather than toward him.
The rightward branch installs the positive horizontal velocity.
Both directions converge to request animation $C and install the upward launch velocity before the sign test.
The delay frames and the un-negated launch share this return.
The cooldown spends one outer loop, rearms the inner counter at three, and steps back two states into the attack preparation rather than to the flight state.
The frames before the cooldown expires return here.
The converter rewrites the record as type $2C4 with a $10-frame timer and a launch whose horizontal component follows the wasp's facing.
The right-facing case keeps the default negative velocity and returns here.
Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs the debris handler, which falls for $10 frames and then raises an explosion, plays SFX $BC and drops a random pickup.
The blink is driven from bit 0 of the timer's low byte, the same pattern the beetle and the shared defeat projectile use.
While the wasp debris timer $48 is active, both retained-bit-7 and cleared-bit-7 blink paths return here; expiration queues SFX $BC before the pickup path with random mask 7.
Shared by the floater and the launcher init states, which call it with d0 set to 0 and 4 respectively, the two record offsets of the parameter table below.

Two four-byte records read as three separate bytes: $18 into $27, then $04 or $02 into $25, then $11 shifted left four into $5A. Only the middle byte differs between the floater and the launcher, so the two enemies share every parameter except that one.
Both the floater and launcher controllers tail-call this routine after dispatching their own states.
It only maps the animation selector at offset 0x5C to one of two sprite mappings and clears the frame counter; it performs no main-state dispatch.
A zero animation request leaves the current mapping in place, which is why both controllers can clear $5C every frame and only the states that want a change write it.
Two long pointers indexed by the animation request less four, so the only legal requests are 4 and 8, which are exactly the values the floater and launcher states write.
Named by Entity_UpdateHandlerTable. State zero skips the defeat checks entirely, so a freshly spawned floater cannot be converted before it has initialised.
The state runs first and the shared animation update second, the same shape the launcher controller uses.
Seven self-relative words measured from the table itself rather than from a base routine.

Seven entries, states $00 to $0C. The floater only ever advances by two from zero and stops at $08, the falling object, which converts itself to a type-$88 effect, so slots $0A and $0C are referenced by the table but never entered.
This is state zero in Enemy_Stage12FloaterStateOffsets and calls the shared sprite initializer before selecting animation state 4.
It creates no projectile and immediately falls through to the player-distance wait state, so it is initialization rather than an attack.
The threshold is a horizontal distance under $60, and the response is an upward $20000, so the floater only starts rising once the player is close.
The far-away frames return here without touching the velocity.
A bare height test: the state advances once Y has risen above $150, with no movement of its own, because the velocity the wait state installed is still in force.
The frames below the threshold return here.

The release waits on a terrain probe returning zero, then installs a $C0 collision byte, an upward $48000, animation 8, and a horizontal velocity taken from the sine table at a random angle and shifted left three, so the scatter direction is random but the speed is not.
Frames blocked by terrain return here and retry on the next one.

Shared by the floater and the launcher tables, at states $08 and $06. The bit-7 test is a byte operation on the top byte of the $1C velocity, so it is a sign test: the object only becomes solid and only checks the lower bound once it is descending.
Both the still-rising frames and the above-the-bound frames return here.
Also entered directly from Projectile_FallingShotInit, so the conversion is shared with a projectile path outside this module.

Named by two tables at once, slot $0A of the floater and slot $08 of the launcher, which is what makes it shared. Neither owner can reach its slot: both enemies advance only by two and stop one slot earlier, at the shared falling object. Its address comes from build/main.lst, because nullsub names carry a counter rather than an address.

Slot $0C of the floater table, two bytes after the shared one, and likewise never entered: no code in this module writes $0C into the state field. It is not orphaned, because the table reference is real. Its address also comes from build/main.lst.
Both the floater and launcher controllers branch here on defeat, inactive-stage state, or collision flags.
The active conversion clears combat fields, installs entity type 0x2D0 and upward falling velocity; it is a shared defeat conversion, not the launcher's main handler.
The active path retypes the object to $2D0, which is index $B4 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable and therefore Enemy_UpdateStage12DefeatDebris, arms a $10-frame fuse and clears the collision bytes.
Entity type 0x2D0, installed by the shared floater/launcher defeat conversion, maps to this handler.
It applies gravity and blinking before the final explosion and pickup, so ownership is shared and the routine is the debris update rather than a launcher-only explosion entry.

The test is whether the object in the Entity57 slot is type $1B8, which is index $6E and so Stage12_YachtControllerMain. While the yacht is present the debris sets bit 4 of its sprite flag byte and drops nothing. That bit is the hide flag: Enemy_Stage12TurretHide writes $10 into the same byte, whose only set bit is bit 4, and every other value this module writes there has it clear.
Bit 7 is set and then cleared again on every frame whose fuse low bit is clear, so the debris flashes at half the frame rate for its $10 frames.

The active Stage 12 debris timer reaches this RTS whether $49 bit zero retains object bit 7 or the fallthrough clears it; expiration instead queues SFX $BC and chooses a pickup with random mask $F or hide from Entity57Type.
It copies the Entity57 position into its own every frame, so the turret rides the yacht rather than the camera, and from state 4 onward it tail-calls the periodic bird spawner.
Seven self-relative words, and unlike the floater dispatcher it does not clear the animation request first, because the turret has no animation.
Seven entries. The reset state writes 6 rather than advancing, so states $06 to $0C form a loop and the turret produces one launcher after another.
The only work is the sprite flag word $0D00 and the advance, so the turret has no position of its own until the controller copies the position of the yacht.
It waits on two conditions: that the Entity57 slot really holds type $1B8, and that the state of that object has reached 6. Only then does it arm the $100-frame delay.
Both failed conditions share this return.
A bare countdown on $48.
The Stage 12 turret delay returns here while timer $48 is nonzero; zero advances controller state.
The state requests one free primary object slot, leaves it dormant as type 0x10, and stores its address at offset 0x4A.
It sets no reload timer or weapon ammunition; the next state later activates that reserved slot as the Stage 12 launcher.
A full object pool leaves the state unchanged, so the allocation is retried every frame until it succeeds.
The only condition compares the turret's own Y coordinate with 0x140; no player object or player position is read.
Once the threshold is reached, the state converts the reserved slot at offset 0x4A to entity type 0x2E4 and initializes its launch delay fields.
The frames before the turret has descended to Y $140 return here, holding the reserved slot dormant at type $10.
Arms a $40-frame gap between launchers.
It writes 6 rather than advancing, which is what closes the launcher production loop.
The Stage 12 turret reset delay returns here while timer $48 is nonzero; zero writes controller state six.
The spawned type is $90, which is index $24 of Entity_UpdateHandlerTable and therefore Enemy_BirdController, not a shot as the former name claimed. The turret is the bird source of the stage.
A one in four draw on the random state picks the $FF frame mask; the other three quarters of the time the $1FF mask halves the rate.
The bird is placed at Y $B0 with $5E set to 1 and no X of its own, so the slot keeps whatever X it had.
Both the off-interval frames and a full object pool return here.
It writes $1000 into the sprite word, whose high byte has only bit 4 set, and that is the same bit the defeat debris sets to suppress its pickup.
Instruction for instruction the floater controller with a different dispatcher, including the same state-zero exemption from the defeat checks.
It shares Enemy_UpdateStage12FloatingAnimation with the floater, which is why both enemies draw from the same two mappings.
Five self-relative words, otherwise identical to the floater dispatcher.
Five entries. The launcher advances by two and stops at $06, the shared falling object, so slot $08 is referenced but never entered, the same situation as the last two slots of the floater table.

It calls the shared sprite init with d0 set to 4, the second parameter record, then overrides the collision bytes and the sprite word with $ED00 and falls straight into the rise state, so the launcher spends no frame in state zero.

The $4E field is both the countdown and the Y offset that Enemy_Stage12LauncherUpdatePosition adds to the yacht position, so decrementing it once a frame walks the launcher from $38 pixels below the yacht up to it, and the state ends exactly when the gap closes. The former wait name described only half of that.
The frames still closing the gap return here.
It reads Entity57, the yacht, not the camera. $4C is the fixed horizontal offset the turret randomised between $50 and $CF, and $4E is the shrinking vertical one.
It keeps following the yacht for another $40 frames, then sets the $40 collision bit, switches the sprite word to $EF00, and leaves with an upward $48000 and a leftward $20000.
The frames before the launch return here, still attached.
The controller fixes its own position, then its state table creates one entity type 0x2D4 and waits until that child changes type before repeating.
Entity type 0x2D4 maps to Enemy_Stage10BeetleController, and no bomber sprite, projectile payload or flight state is initialized.
Four self-relative words naming the wave controller's init, spawn, wait and delay states.
The controller is pinned to a fixed position every frame by its caller, and this state only installs the invisible flag word before advancing.
The state allocates a child, installs entity type 0x2D4 and places it at one of two screen-edge X coordinates with a small random Y offset.
The installed type dispatches to the beetle controller, so this is a beetle-wave spawn state rather than a bomber projectile spawn.
One random bit decides the entry side, placing the new beetle at X $78 here or at $1C8 on the other branch.
A failed slot allocation returns here and the spawn is retried next frame.
The controller keeps the spawned record's address in $4C and waits until that record's type word stops being $2D4, which happens when the beetle converts itself to debris.
Every frame the beetle is still alive returns here.
After a $40-frame gap the controller returns to the spawn state, so the wave is a single beetle at a time rather than a group.
The frames before the gap expires return here.
The controller removes itself instead of respawning when the shared entity slot holds type $1B8, which is the special-stage variant of this sequence.
The setup reads three bytes from Enemy_Stage10BeetleSpriteParameters at the caller's index and scales the last by sixteen into field $5A, the same shape the circling-enemy setup uses.
One three-byte record packed into two words; only index zero is ever passed.

Entity_UpdateHandlerTable installs this handler. It converts the beetle to debris on negative health or when the stage spawn countdown expires, and otherwise steps the random generator once per frame.
After the state runs, the facing is taken from the sign of the horizontal velocity, and a zero vertical velocity restores the walking animation, so the walk resumes automatically after every bounce.
Airborne frames keep their current animation and return here.
